#3653. Pedro Almodóvar Didn’t Think He Could Write a Novel. But Once He Started, the “Story Began to Pour Out”

A woman who might, or might not, be Penélope Cruz stares down at us from the wall. For now, I’ll accept that it is Cruz because the image is on a poster for Broken Embraces, a 2009 film she starred in. My hesitation in believing it’s her, however, is because finding a resemblance between the woman on the poster and Cruz requires a lot of generosity. It’s as if the artist had painted her based on a detailed description he’d heard, but he’d never actually seen his subject onscreen. “We were given this in India,” explains Pedro Almodóvar’s brother, Agustín, the head and owner of El Deseo, the production company behind Almodóvar’s films. “Specialized artists still hand-paint their movie posters, and the results are images like this.” The work’s imperfections give it a charm that no poster created by AI could ever match.

This brings to mind one of the stories in Almodóvar’s first novel, The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes. It depicts a Blade Runner–style dystopian future where replicants, jaded by digital perfection, are fascinated by the rough edges of human culture. The book has just been published in Spain (it is scheduled to be published in the United States, in Spanish, in February 2027), following the release of Almodóvar’s latest film, Bitter Christmas (which will be in select US theaters on November 13, and released nationwide on November 25).

Both works have much in common: They are works of autofiction with protagonists—the filmmakers played by Bárbara Lennie and Leonardo Sbaraglia in the film, and a very multifaceted character named Flavio Guijarro in the book—who appear to be alternative versions of their creator. At the same time, they are clearly different from Almodóvar, like the difference between Cruz and the woman on the Indian movie poster.

I ask Almodóvar why he decided to recount Flavio’s story in the form of a novel rather than a movie, but he appears to have not heard my question and answers instead as if I’d asked him why it took him so long to publish a novel, which is undoubtedly much more interesting: “I think the reason I hadn’t written a novel until now was that I wasn’t sure I’d be able to, even though I’d wanted to write one since I was a young man. At first, however, I didn’t even know myself that this story would be a novel. I started with a simple anecdote about an acting coach and an actor, and that opened the floodgates; the story began to pour out. When it was already over 30 pages, I sent it to my editor. He told me there was a novel there and that I should keep going.”

The 77-year-old director from La Mancha poses in a jacket, polo shirt, pants, and sneakers by Loewe.

He will answer many other questions that I haven’t asked but should have: “I didn’t know, for example, that I’d include my story ‘Addiction,’ which is a little treat for fans that had already appeared in Pain and Glory. It was going to be a monologue that Carmen Machi would perform in a small theater, but I ended up giving it to Asier Etxeandia in that film. I also wrote Pain and Glory very quickly. And in it, I inserted, like little snippets, more pieces that I’d already written. For example, there’s another story, just five pages long, about a chance encounter with an actor with whom I’d had a very bad relationship in the past [Eusebio Poncela, who starred in Law of Desire 40 years ago] and with whom, in the story, I ended up doing heroin. In real life, the fact that he was using heroin while we were filming was the reason we had a falling out. Thanks to those preexisting elements, which fit into the story, I was able to write that movie so quickly. And the same is true of my new book. What defines it is a sense of absolute freedom.”

And maybe that sentence is, in the end, the answer to all my questions for Almodóvar.

Vanity Fair España: Is that sense of freedom why you decided to write a novel instead of a screenplay?

Pedro Almodóvar: In Bitter Christmas, Leonardo Sbaraglia’s character says he needs absolute freedom to work. Just like me throughout my entire career. That freedom feels more intense with a novel because it’s a format with which I have less experience. I’ve woven it together from different stories, but they all revolve around the protagonist and it’s been very satisfying. It wasn’t a whim: The book has the same rigor to it as everything else I do, but that freedom is deeply rooted in my style. That’s why I wrote it so quickly. Everything flowed naturally.

There is a tradition of using a novel as a container for many stories, as with Don Quixote or Jan Potocki’s The Manuscript Found in Saragossa. On the other hand, speaking of influences, it’s interesting that when you wrote your Patty Diphusa stories in 1983 [included in Patty Diphusa and Other Writings, published by Faber & Faber in 1992], Anita Loos and pornographic photo novels are influences that appear in the mix, but in The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes, you turn to, let’s say, more distinguished names: Henry James, Nabokov, and Colm Tóibín, who even appears as a character.

I’m not trying to compare myself to Cervantes or Potocki, but yes, that’s what the book is. That’s precisely why this novel can’t be adapted for the screen: You’d have to choose one part of it and develop it, but as it stands now, that wouldn’t be possible. Those earlier influences are still with me—Anita Loos is certainly among them—and they continue to inspire me with both specific phrases and broader themes. In the novel, I name authors who inspire me and with whom I connect organically, such as Joan Didion and Virginia Woolf. But Patty and Flavio have something in common: a sense of urgency that drives them to write at a breakneck pace, out of a physiological need. Neither of them sleeps much, though in Patty’s case it’s because she can’t stop doing cocaine. Beyond that, other differences set them apart, including the differences between what life was like in the ’80s and what it’s like now.

What sort of differences are there, and where are they most apparent?

Take sex, for example. Patty Diphusa is an archetype of the 1980s, a time of absolute freedom in Spain, and her character can only be understood in the context of the utterly carefree and hedonistic lifestyle we led back then. If she sucks a guy's dick in a bathroom, she’ll then record her wild thoughts because she considers herself a sort of philosopher of eroticism. Although Flavio is a very free-spirited person, just like the book itself, he belongs to another era and another generation. Here, sex is part of a love story, and his attitude toward it is very different. I devote less space to the erotic scenes in this book because I assume people already know what it’s like to sleep with someone.

Almodóvar, in another room at El Deseo’s headquarters, wearing a Louis Vuitton jacket and a Prada knit polo shirt.

You’ve argued on different occasions that in the 1980s, many people in Spain chose that hedonistic and seemingly frivolous lifestyle as a reaction to the previous era, and that this was a political statement. Now we see a new generation adopting a different kind of stance. For example, all across Europe, people are taking to the streets to demand their right to housing and decent living conditions, and there’s not much frivolity in that. How do you interpret this change?

I completely empathize with and support the people filling the streets. They are demanding fundamental rights that are enshrined in the Spanish constitution and which are now in jeopardy: housing, health care, and education. I went to the encampment on the Puerta del Sol [in Madrid] only a few times, because I was in New York presenting Bitter Christmas at the New York Film Festival and also because I think a famous person doesn’t really fit in at these demonstrations—if we go, we distort the spirit of it. But I did go, and I bought them food because that’s what I thought they’d need, even though they told me they’d be better off with some tables. I don’t just support their initiative; I’m glad it happened. One thing I’d heard about young people, a generation I don’t know much about, was from a news article that said that 25% of young Spaniards wouldn’t mind living under a dictatorship like Franco’s. I shuddered. What happened in the Puerta del Sol shows that there’s a whole crowd of young people beyond those who go to Ferraz to pray the rosary [since November 2023, a group of Catholic protesters has gathered daily to pray outside the headquarters of the PSOE, Spain’s socialist party, on Madrid’s Calle Ferraz]. They aren’t rich, and they don’t have their lives figured out; they can’t work in the professions they studied to pursue, and they don’t earn enough money to buy homes. That’s terrifying. And the political parties have shown their true colors when it comes to housing. Of course, the PSOE is late to the game with the so-called Maricarmen decrees [a series of measures named after Maricarmen Abascal, whose eviction from her home and subsequent death in October galvanized activists], but at least it has reacted. The starkly different reactions from the Partido Popular [Popular Party] and Vox [center-right and far-right parties, respectively] already tell you what they think about this issue.

Would you agree today with that line from Gloria Muñoz in The Flower of My Secret: “With so much reality, the country’s ready to explode”?

She was talking in literary terms, but it’s true that this phrase has taken on a life of its own over time and has spilled over into other areas. The same thing has happened to another phrase: “A woman is more authentic the more she resembles the person she has dreamed of becoming,” as Agrado said in All About My Mother. It was a line written for a transgender woman, and one that makes perfect sense for her. But now it can be understood in relation to any kind of character: It speaks to authenticity, to staying true to oneself and to one’s own dreams. In the case of young people in our country, we’re talking about a social reality. The country has changed a lot, and we’re very polarized—though France is even worse off than Spain. Europe is in very bad shape overall. The kind of news coverage being produced plays a major role in this rise of the far right. Since the images promoted by the right are so jarring and sensationalist, TV stations pick up on them, and in doing so, they’re effectively promoting figures like Vito Quiles [a far-right activist and influencer]. Damn it, don’t put Vito Quiles on TV—it’s better if we don’t even know where he is or what he’s doing!

Are you particularly concerned about the attention that the far right is getting?

People like [Santiago] Abascal [president of the Vox political party] and [Javier]Milei [president of Argentina] want to do away with the state. Milei, the biggest loudmouth of them all, even aims to destroy the state from within the state itself, which is diabolical. I cite Milei as an example because he says so himself. And on top of that, people elect him for that very reason: He’s someone who has come to power democratically, just like [Donald] Trump. So we’re putting the tools of democracy in the hands of someone whose main goal is to destroy it. Furthermore, in a world so polarized—and with a far right that has no qualms about calling itself fascist—the emergence of AI creates a perfect storm.

One of the stories in your book is, in fact, a dystopian tale inspired by Blade Runner, in which large corporations with shadowy agendas seek to create a less human world. You have contributed so much to human creativity. Are you concerned about how that creativity is being taken over by AI?

I’m always open to change. It’s necessary for society to move forward. But I think the encroachment of AI on human agency is terrible. They should start regulating it now. I’m concerned about the jobs it will replace and also the synthetic culture it will create. In fact, a synthetic culture based on data already exists, and it lacks a soul. The genesis of a screenplay must be human, because AI doesn’t have the sense of doubt, the patience, or the capacity for stories to build up layers of meaning, as in Talk to Her and Bad Education. We need a society that cares about culture, promotes it, and supports it, and not a soulless culture focused only on the immediate. I haven’t used AI creatively, nor do I really know how to. But I’m concerned that we’re now unable to tell whether an image is real or not, given the level of perfection this technology has reached. And moreover, behind it all are very powerful people who know no limits.

On another topic, standards of beauty have changed, with cosmetic surgery and fillers now widely prevalent. For someone who places such importance on the expressions of actors that must also be a cause for concern.

Well, I wouldn’t mind if an actor in one of my movies had had plastic surgery. For example, I wouldn’t turn down Nicole Kidman for that reason—she’s not only a great actor, but she has also had plastic surgery, and she looks better than ever. Because, these days, actors who’ve had plastic surgery are part of the landscape. It’s so common that you no longer have to explain that a character has had it done; it’s accepted as a matter of course. What’s more, cosmetic surgery has advanced so much that high-profile figures who’ve had work done—like Donatella Versace, Lindsay Lohan, or Nicole Kidman herself—have completely erased the signs of their previous procedures with splendid results. [Editor’s note: Lindsay Lohan has denied having a facelift, while Kidman has never confirmed undergoing any plastic surgery.] The big problem is that, if you make films set in the past, you can’t cast women with plastic surgery or lip fillers; it would be anachronistic, just like putting a piece of furniture from the 1980s in a film about the Spanish Civil War. But it’s true that in my films, plastic surgery hasn’t usually been an option, for aesthetic reasons. Fortunately, there will always be people like Frances McDormand and Carmen Maura. We need older women who look their age.

What interests me most about your new novel is the protagonist’s relationship with an actor, Alez Mazado—a sex symbol who isn’t very intelligent but has a certain natural talent and is open to being molded. Flavio is his Pygmalion. There’s even an explicit reference to Hitchcock’s film Vertigo, which also features that kind of relationship. Do you often have that kind of dynamic with your actors?

I’m like Jimmy Stewart in Vertigo: With actors, I get involved in their hair, lip color, outfits—everything. When I watched Vertigo for the umpteenth time, I thought that character was a director: “He knows exactly what he wants,” they tell him when he takes Kim Novak to try on outfits at a store. The actors I work with and I have adapted to each other, just like in a marriage—in my films, they speak differently; the actors themselves say so. Aitana Sánchez-Gijón told me that she felt she could do anything after playing her role in Bitter Christmas. But I work differently with each actor. With Penélope, for example, I rehearse a lot, and the more we rehearse, the better she gets; then I shoot many takes, and the 10th one is better than the third. And if I can shoot 12, even better. But others don’t like to rehearse, like Antonio Banderas, because he’s a different kind of actor. He has extraordinary intuition and instinct. I don’t need to talk to him as much or push him so hard.

People talk about Los Javis [the moniker for actors turned directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo] as your natural heirs, in the wake of the success of La Bola Negra, which you coproduced through El Deseo. Do you think they will continue your creative legacy?

They definitely treat me like their mentor. They know entire films of mine by heart, even lines that I don’t remember. They’ve been deeply influenced by my films, just as I’ve been influenced by [Luis García] Berlanga, [Rafael] Azcona, [Luis] Buñuel, and [Carlos] Saura. Even if you don’t want to admit it, everyone has role models. I find it flattering, but to say they’re my heirs is to minimize their work. They have a style all their own. In fact, if I were to write the screenplay for La Bola Negra, it would be very different. I don’t feel like their father. I take responsibility for my films and nothing else.

How do you view their film’s unstoppable run at the awards and at the box office?

Los Javis are the big thing right now. Their film is going to be the highest-grossing Spanish movie of all time, although I don’t remember how much The Last Torch Song (1957), starring Sara Montiel, made back in the day. At El Deseo, we’ve had two fantastic years—first with Oliver Laxe’s film [Sirāt], which we also coproduced, and now this one. And I hope the Javis can keep on going and make it through the rest of their promotional tour and then the awards season. From my experience as an Oscar nominee, I know the best moment isn’t when they call your name, but when the ceremony ends. That’s when your life is your own again—whether to start on the next project or simply sleep if that’s what you prefer.

Have you shared that experience with the Javis? Do you give them advice?

Just yesterday I texted Javier Ambrossi, and he told me they’ve already had enough. And they have no idea what’s still in store for them! We’ll meet next week, and I’ll explain it all to him. At the Oscars, they’re the favorites in the best-international-feature-film category; they’re a sure thing. Although I experienced that curse of being the front-runner when Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown was the favorite and then Pelle the Conqueror ended up winning—a film no one even remembers now. But anyway, everyone now expects La Bola Negra to be nominated in other categories as well, which is historic for our film industry. It’s great for us.

On a recent podcast, one of the actors from La Bola Negra, Yenesi, described the film as Federico García Lorca fan fiction—which is actually quite fitting, since its entire narrative is built on elements related to Lorca’s life and writings. Roland Barthes had already spoken of the death of the author, and Eugenio d’Ors famously said, “There is no true originality outside tradition. Everything that is not tradition is plagiarism.”

I’ve written that phrase down! I read it in one of [journalist and writer Francisco] Umbral’s columns; I suppose he got it from d’Ors.

In other words, Umbral appropriated it for himself, and in doing so, he proved its enduring relevance.

It’s inevitable that the things you like will influence your work. And the things you hate too. When you write, you have a general idea of the story, but as you develop it, what you create is rooted in things that are part of your life. And your life always resembles the things you’ve seen before. I’m fascinated by the phenomenon of fan fiction because of its contradictory nature; it’s a miracle that an entire culture has developed around this phenomenon, which exists outside the mainstream market yet at the same time feeds off the most mainstream works, such as Star Trek or Star Wars. Fan fiction is a declaration of love for the original and proof that great stories never end: There will always be someone to continue them. Just as people don’t die as long as there’s someone who remembers them.

Of course I have to ask you, with the promotional tour for Bitter Christmas coming to an end, what are you working on next?

Well, it was going to be a comedy, but after I finished it, even though I was 90% passionate about it, I realized there was something about the supporting characters that I didn’t like. So I’ve put it on hold, as I’ve done before with other projects. And now I’m writing something else. I’m well into it, but I can’t say anything. They’ll kill me if I do. It’ll be based on a book, and we’re currently working out the rights. This one will have plenty of humor too. Because I know for sure that, after Bitter Christmas, I don’t want to talk about myself anymore. I need different characters. And humor too.

Is there any movie you wish you’d made but that’s missing from your filmography?

There are several recent films I would have loved to have made. For example, Drive My Car by Ryusuke Hamaguchi and Anatomy of a Fall by Justine Triet. Or Sentimental Value by Joachim Trier. I mean, I should have made that movie! It has everything: the cinema, a house, a father and his daughters. Everything.

Should we just accept, by the way, that you won’t make your own movie about the Spanish Civil War? Or was Parallel Mothers already your take on it?

When I read Cosamala, Alana S. Portero’s latest book, I really wanted to adapt it. But it’s such a wonderful work of literature that translating it into images would greatly diminish the wonder and surprise of her writing. If the book proves anything, it’s that Alana is a tremendous writer. I’d have to find another angle from which to tell the story of the civil war. But I do want to do it.

Visuals Editor and Director: Reyes Domínguez. Art Direction: Ángel Perea. Production: Lucía Pregigueiro. Hair and Makeup: @tuozzoli (Kasteel Artist Management) for @oribe. Photography Assistants: Isra Lozano and Ayub El Kadmiri. Styling Assistants: Juan Luis Ascanio and Renata Ito.

This interview was originally published by Vanity Fair España. It was translated by John Newton.

#3652. Why Wyatt Callow From The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Looks So Familiar

Lionsgate's "Hunger Games" films series is an anomaly among franchises. Ever since its main story ended, the property has only gotten bigger and better thanks to prequel movies that have expanded its world, all while deepening the characters we already knew and introducing new ones that folks have come to love. Indeed, it's those very elements that have allowed these films to set themselves apart from all the other "Hunger Games"-style movies out there.

The latest "Hunger Games" film, "Sunrise on the Reaping," is arguably the bleakest and meanest entry in the franchise yet. The "Hunger Games" equivalent of the fantastic "Star Wars" series "Andor," it tells a devastating tale about loss, sacrifice, and people who don't know if they'll ever get to see victory or freedom. As /Film's review puts it, "Beyond the shock value, this story remains human, emotional, and gripping from beginning to end."

At the same time, "Sunrise on the Reaping" is very much a prequel. In addition to its many callbacks to previous "Hunger Games" movies (including 2023's "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes"), it's full of younger versions of well-known characters like Effie Trinket and Caesar Flickerman (as played here by Elle Fanning and Kieran Culkin, respectively). But above all else, it's a story that reveals how a young Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) survived his own horrifying set of Games.

Joining Haymitch on his journey are his fellow District 12 tributes, among them Ben Wang as Wyatt Callow. Wang, as it were, has quickly made a name for himself, appearing in everything from the sequel "Karate Kid: Legends" to the devastating Stephen King adaptation "The Long Walk" (as was directed by longtime "Hunger Games" helmsman Francis Lawrence). And by the look of things, the actor's career will only continue to flourish in the near-future.

After scoring a small part in an episode of the "MacGyver" reboot series, Ben Wang landed the lead role in the short-lived but well-received Disney+ series "American Born Chinese" (which has some very cool action scenes and a killer cast). Around that same time, he also appeared in the feature film adaptation of the "Mean Girls" stage musical.

Still, it was really the one-two punch of 2025's "Karate Kid: Legends" (pun kinda intended) and "The Long Walk" that proved Wang could be a star. The former, in particular, showed the young actor could go toe to toe with "Karate Kid" franchise veterans Ralph Macchio and Jackie Chan while still shining on his own merits. What's more, it allowed him to earn his action movie bonafides, as he does more than his fair share of convincing stunt work in the film.

Then came the emotionally obliterating all-time great Stephen King adaptation that is "The Long Walk," in which Wang delivers a harrowing and heart-wrenching performance — making it the perfect prelude to his turn in "Sunrise on the Reaping." And while there's not much action in the movie, it's an equally dark dystopian work in which kids compete to the death to try and better their lots in life.

Ultimately, Wang doesn't have a huge role in "Sunrise on the Reaping," but he makes the most of his screen time, depicting Wyatt as an oddsmaker desperate to demonstrate he can control his own life and beat the odds in the games. Up next, the actor will co-star in the sixth and final season of Apple TV's acclaimed sci-fi series "For All Mankind" before joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe as Iceman in a new "X-Men" film.

It's an honor to be the answer to a question on Jeopardy!, and I'd assume it's an even higher honor to be the answer for Final Jeopardy! So, with that in mind, it's always fun to see how people react to being the subject of a question featured on the show. Case in point: Ice-T had a very funny take when he found out that someone didn't know he was the answer to Final Jeopardy!.

Final Jeopardy! can literally make or break someone’s future on the long-running game show. The clues can range from history to literature to, yes, even pop culture. On the episode from the 2026 TV schedule that aired on October 28, Ice-T was the answer for the final round. Two people got it right, but one person was wrong. Ice-T addressed the moment while appearing on the Today Show and revealed just what he thinks of the whole ordeal:

I’m in a lot of crossword puzzles, because Ice-T, I-C-E-T, is a weird spelled thing. But Jeopardy, I’ve been in Jeopardy before, but Final Jeopardy. …. [They asked] who put out an album, Home Invasion, and also is the longest-running character in television. And the guy said Tim Allen. I think he was thinking about Home Improvement, right? But the two women got it right, and I only care about the women [laughs]. So, you know, he lost, and they won. But that’s how it goes. But Final Jeopardy!’s a big deal.

Of course, being a clue on Jeopardy! is a big deal, even if it does sting when someone does not know the answer. And as Ice-T pointed out, he’s been in plenty of clues over the years. That being said, it’s a lot different when you’re in Final Jeopardy!

Overall, I love that Ice-T wasn’t too hurt over being mistaken for Tim Allen, and instead focused on the fact that the two women got it right, which is all he cares about. I'm also very entertained by the image of Tim Allen trying to rap.

Anyway, the clue was for the category “Current TV Streaks,” and it just shows that even if a clue seems easy, it may not be for a lot of people. For host Ken Jennings, there was one category that made him nervous when he was competing, and it was surprisingly hockey. While he wound up being one of the biggest Jeopardy! winners of all time and no one has yet to beat his 74-game streak, it sounds like that still haunts him. So, everyone has their blind spots.

Meanwhile, that Final Jeopardy! clue made me realize something truly insane. Despite the fact that Law & Order: SVU is in its 28th season, it’s wild to me that Ice-T has been playing Odafin “Fin” Tutuola for almost three decades. He’s been on the NBC drama since the second season and is one of the longest-running actors in the Law & Order franchise. Luckily, he doesn’t have any plans to leave any time soon. While he has been worried that he’d be written out as the show has had to make room for Kellie Giddish, that has not been the case.

Hopefully, the next time Ice-T is an answer for Final Jeopardy! everyone gets it right. However, even if it’s just the women, I’m sure he will be just fine. In the meantime, fans can catch him on Law & Order: SVU on Thursday, December 3, at 9 p.m. ET on NBC, streaming the next day with a Peacock subscription.

#3650. Matt Damon Reveals the Surprising Secret Behind 'The Odyssey's Epic Final Battle

Hundreds of choreographed moves, veteran stunt performers, and a little improvisation helped bring the film's climactic scene to life.

When Odysseus (Matt Damon) finally returns home in Homer's Odyssey, he discovers that getting back to Ithaca was only half the battle. His palace has been overrun by suitors hoping to marry his wife, Penelope (Anne Hathaway), and claim his kingdom. Naturally, Odysseus isn't particularly thrilled about any of this. What follows is one of the epic poem's most memorable confrontations, as the Greek hero takes matters into his own hands.

Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey brings that showdown to the screen in a climactic fight that required an extraordinary amount of choreography. But according to Damon, the secret to pulling off the sequence wasn't memorizing a complex choreography. Instead, it was surrounding himself with stunt performers skilled enough to adapt to whatever he did.

Speaking with Polygon ahead of the film's home release, Damon and co-star John Leguizamo discussed the sequence, which Leguizamo watched being filmed. The experience left him wishing he had some popcorn so he could sit back and enjoy the spectacle.

For Leguizamo, watching Damon take on the suitors was one of the production's standout experiences. He even got permission to remove the special contact lenses designed to portray him as the blind swineherd Eumaeus so he could really observe the action. "There were a few times when they'd let me not wear the contacts and just hang out," Leguizamo tells Polygon. "I walked on set when he [Damon] was doing the fight sequences at the end, when he took down all the suitors. That was incredible to watch. It was like watching a Kurosawa samurai movie."

Leguizamo wasn't part of the fight, but he had a front-row seat as Damon and the stunt team brought the elaborate sequence to life.

"It was so amazing," Leguizamo continues. "I wanted to have popcorn and just watch it over and over again."

The comparison to legendary Japanese filmmaker Akira Kurosawa is particularly fitting given the director's influence on generations of action filmmakers. But Damon is quick to point out that much of the credit should go to the people he was fighting.

"They had the best stunt team," Damon says, singling out stunt coordinator George Cottle.

According to Damon, the production benefited from an unusual situation in Los Angeles. With fewer productions underway, highly experienced stunt professionals were available to work on the film, including performers who ordinarily operated at the stunt coordinator level.

"Because there's not a lot of work in Los Angeles, there were all of these people who were coordinator-level stunt people who were available to come in and play those roles," Damon says. "And a lot of the suitors are around my age. They're older. So these are stunt guys who are incredible, enormously experienced, and really good."

That experience proved essential once the cameras started rolling. Stunt fighting isn't simply about memorizing a series of punches, blocks, and movements. It's a collaborative process that requires the performers to respond to one another.

"I've always thought stunt fighting is like dancing, really," Damon says. He also acknowledges that he wasn't necessarily the most accomplished dancer in the group. "When one, me, isn't as good a dancer, it gets made up for by the other being an expert."

Rather than expecting Damon to execute every movement with the precision of a professional stunt performer, the team could adjust its timing and positioning around him.

"I could move through these sequences, because these guys were adjusting in real time to my movement and my spacing," Damon says. "And if I was off, they could recalibrate and still make it work."

That level of experience was especially important given the sheer amount of choreography involved.

"How many moves did you have? Did you count them?" Leguizamo asks.

"I have no idea," Damon replies. "It was a lot. It was hundreds of moves."

"They must have been over a hundred," Leguizamo agrees.

"These guys were just so great," Damon concludes. "That really made that sequence what it was."

#3648. The Rings Of Power Season 3 References The Most Powerful Dragon In Lord Of The Rings History

Spoilers ahead for Episodes 5 and 6 of "The Rings of Power" Season 3.

As a "Lord of the Rings" prequel, "The Rings of Power" takes an interesting approach. Sure, when you think about it, the show doesn't always fit into he greater "Lord of the Rings" canon, and it sometimes introduces elements that threaten to change the larger franchise as we know it. At the same time, it has some pretty cool ideas, whether it's the creation of Mount Doom from Season 1 or Sauron (Charlie Vickers) meeting a Balrog (Simon Pegg) in Season 3. Overall, the series knows how to capitalize on the vastness of J. R. R. Tolkien's literary source material to imagine new concepts for a different medium.

But perhaps one of the most fascinating aspects of "The Rings of Power" is how its writers have been able to reference material from "The Silmarillion" — in particular, where it concerns the First Age of Middle-earth — despite Amazon not having the rights to adapt the book. Not only that, the show has alluded to plot points from that work on more than one occasion, be it Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards) being jealous that he's unable to match the craft of the legendary Fëanor or the continuous allusions to Morgoth being Sauron's former boss.

"The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 5 even name-drops a First Age legend when Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) tells Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) exactly how he was captured so many centuries ago. As it turns out, he was taken in after Ancalagon the Black — the most powerful dragon in Middle-earth's history — set his entire legion ablaze, with Sauron astride. The only reason Celeborn survived was because he was kicked off his horse and into some water, shielding him from the inferno.

Ancalagon the Black has never appeared on-screen, but his legacy is legendary. In J.R.R. Tolkien's literature, dragons were specifically bred by Morgoth, first as terrestrial lizards, but later as winged monsters. Ancalagon was known as the Great Dragon of Morgoth, the largest winged dragon in the history of Middle-Earth. He is described by Tolkien as being "as tall as a mountain" and was the leader of the great host of winged dragons that Morgoth unleashed during the War of Wrath in the First Age. The great beast only serves one purpose in the larger Legendarium — to be Morgoth's ultimate weapon of war, one so terrible it nearly ruined the Valar.

Ancalagon is by far the largest dragon in fiction and is much, much larger than any of the dragons in George R.R. Martin's "Game of Thrones" stories, the massive Balerion the Dread included. But unlike Balerion, Ancalagon didn't really do much. Indeed, in Tolkien's canon, he basically appeared for about a day, driving back the Valar until Eärendil arrived with his flying ship and an army of eagles led by their king, Thorondor. Eärendil and the eagles then battled Ancalagon and the dragons for a day and night, only for Eärendil to eventually overthrow the great dragon and cast him into the volcanoes of Thangorodrim (where Morgoth's fortress lay).

The death of Ancalagon also marked the end of the War of Wrath in Middle-earth. And even though the race survived, as evidenced by the later existence of dragons like Smaug, they never reached the heights of the Great Dragon again. Anyway, there's something for you to keep in your back pocket as you continue making your way through "The Rings of Power" on Prime Video.

#3647. Luca Guadagnino and Andrew Garfield Get Real About 'Artificial'

Ask a large language model the same question twice, and you will get two different answers. Like this one: Have Andrew Garfield and Sam Altman ever met?

In an interview with Vanity Fair global editorial director Mark Guiducci this fall, Altman claimed he waved to Garfield while Garfield was shooting Luca Guadagnino’s new film, Artificial, near Altman’s house. Garfield—who plays Altman in the movie—remembers things differently.

“All I know is that I was looking out for him on that day when we were shooting. I was really looking out for him,” Garfield tells me in October, shortly after Artificial’s premiere at the New York Film Festival. “And I was looking at every single tinted car window. I was looking in the windows of the house. I was checking to see the security guard. No, I didn’t see him. I wish I had.”

It’s a question that reverberates both through and around Artificial. From the start, the film has been an intriguing mash-up: a marriage between cinema’s great sensualist and the nerd kingdom of Silicon Valley. Artificial tells the story of the OpenAI CEO’s rise and fall and rise; it was cast and shot in record time to keep pace with the drumbeat of AI doomsday headlines. Then the movie became the headlines after Amazon MGM abruptly dropped Artificial from its slate—a few months after the studio’s parent company, Amazon, invested $50 billion in OpenAI.

A24 declined to rescue Artificial. So did Netflix, Focus Features, and Clockwork, the new specialty arm of Warner Bros. Finally, the lightning bolt of a feature got picked up by Neon, the distributor that’s won six consecutive Palmes d’Or at Cannes.

The film’s electric relationship to the very recent past makes it the most zeitgeist-nailing tech blockbuster since The Social Network. The difference is that back in 2010, Facebook was where you made friends on the internet. Artificial, by contrast, is a film about a self-teaching, self-aware robot that’s getting smarter by the minute and might destroy the human world. And it’s happening in real time.

“You see, we were very prescient with things,” Guadagnino tells me. “I know my subject. I studied my subject very, very much.”

HERE TO MAKE FRIENDS Artificial ends with a heartbreaking act of betrayal—but Guadagnino, Borisov, and Garfield left the project with their bond intact.

Artificial also has a button-pushing relationship with the truth as it endeavors to tell the real story of how OpenAI was born and investigate how reliable the people behind OpenAI are. If Altman can’t be trusted with small details—about, say, whether he ever aimed a friendly wave at Garfield—can he be trusted with the most important technology of our time?

“I question the validity of his statement about being there while we were filming,” Monica Barbaro, who plays former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati in the film, tells me. “I mean, we don’t know if that’s true. And that feels textbook to me.”

In 2024, Amazon bought a script by Simon Rich about Sam Altman and the formation of OpenAI—one of many ChatGPT-related projects then getting passed around town. Rich’s take had the backing of hit-churning producer David Heyman—the man behind Paddington and the Harry Potter series—and his script pulled no punches. To write it, Rich mined details from a childhood friend who had a job at OpenAI (and, as of now, still works there). By the end of the process, Rich was terrified of the power his friend’s colleagues commanded.

“I came up with this last-ditch effort to warn mankind,” Rich said. He’s a comedy writer, but here he isn’t joking. “And I hope to God that it helps people pay attention.”

After shopping the film around to directors, the studio landed on Guadagnino. To some, the Call Me by Your Name director seemed like a strange choice for a film about scientists, coders, and start-up bros. The director barely uses AI himself, or even thinks about it.

ARTIFICIAL RECKONING Garfield’s first thought when reading Artificial was, It’s Luca doing The Social Network.

“I think we should not let ourselves give AI such an important role. I think for me, AI is a prop, a gadget,” Guadagnino tells me. “Definitely AI has high-end worth [for], I don’t know, the military, medicine. But in general, as a sort of everyday life usage of AI, I think it’s just a little gadget. And I don’t believe that we should ever consider the possibility that it can equal whatever we can do as people.”

Garfield approached the material from a different vantage. By the time he got his hands on the script, the actor had been deeply invested in the Silicon Valley origin-story mythos for years—ever since he starred in that other major movie about a world-changing digital platform. His first thought when reading Artificial was, It’s Luca doing The Social Network. “And I thought, Oh my God,” says the actor, sitting in a suite at the Carlyle Hotel. But the movie also had its own gloss. “Simon’s script was so funny—like a stone being skimmed a thousand times across, and then a couple of really deep dives in the midst.”

Making Artificial would allow Garfield to scratch an old itch. “In The Social Network, I was auditioning for [Mark] Zuckerberg. Then they found Jesse [Eisenberg],” who was much better for the role, Garfield says. “But it left this little dangling thread, because I started to imagine how I would play Zuckerberg: how I would try and enter that ambition and that drive and that responsibility. A kind of ability to make huge global decisions that are going to have potentially really positive effects on humanity, but inevitably, really, really heavily negative effects on humanity.”

THE ENGINEER “I feel myself a little bit like Ilya during interviews,” says Borisov.

Garfield is not actually the lead in Artificial. The movie is focused less on Altman than on slightly naive genius coder Ilya Sutskever, played heroically by Oscar nominee Yura Borisov. Borisov has definitively never met the man he’s depicting in the film. But from afar, he can relate to Sutskever. Neither of them is quite comfortable in the spotlight.

“I feel myself a little bit like Ilya during interviews because I’m every time very...I know what to say because I feel a lot about this,” the Russian actor says from a couch at the Carlyle next to Garfield. “I can see the same in his public speeches, because I’m really nervous during some public stuff.”

Though there’s a translator next to him, Borisov soldiers through the interview with just one request for a lifeline. He adds that by cosmic coincidence, he and Sutskever have the same birthday.

Guadagnino was fully aware of the breakneck clip of the developing OpenAI saga. He cast his leads in days and began shooting the film in late July 2025. Artificial wrapped just two months later. As he spent the winter hunkered down in the editing room, word about the film got out. While Rich’s original script was hardly a puff piece, rumor had it that the final film leaned even harder into a negative portrayal of Altman.

There’s no proof that a Jeff Bezos deal had any direct effect on decisions made by Bezos’s movie studio. But for whatever reason, late last spring, Guadagnino learned Amazon would be cutting the film loose.

All of a sudden, the speedily assembled project was in a holding pattern. The trades speculated that Amazon was deliberately killing the film to protect Altman; others wondered if the movie was being dropped not due to a conflict of interest but because it hadn’t played well in early screenings.

Barbaro pushes back on that notion. “I did believe in Luca and the film, and I had already heard really positive things from people who had seen it—really interesting positive reviews,” she says. “There is a thing these companies can do—any production company—which is to essentially build the release and squash a film. And Amazon is not a company that I think necessarily needs to make its money back on an investment like this.”

Either way, it was unclear if Artificial would ever see the light of day. “It’s a dialogue between our fields: tech and art,” Borisov says. “And I don’t know what sells, what will happen. It’s unpredictable.”

In the end, the film was picked up by Neon—an outcome Garfield finds surprising for a few reasons. “I felt very impressed that Amazon wanted to make the film, and very impressed again when they decided [that while] they didn’t want to release it, they didn’t kill it,” he says. He pauses for a second. “They could have killed it.”

Garfield’s thrilled about the film’s eventual home too. Neon, he says pointedly, is “a place for artists to be free artists.” Guadagnino feels similarly, though he claims to have zero ill will toward the studio that threw his movie to the wolves.

“I had went through a process with Amazon that I loved. They were fantastic in making this movie with me. I owe them a lot,” says Guadagnino, who’d done four films with the studio prior to Artificial: Bones and All, Challengers, Suspiria, and After the Hunt.

But what was it like to watch his film fall into limbo while the trades salivated over its demise? Here too, Guadagnino is blissfully zen: “Once the thing happened, I deferred to the thing. Meaning if that was the case, that was the case.”

Even after watching the film twice, I am still pleasantly surprised that Artificial actually exists in the world—that Guadagnino was able to capture the man-child bonhomie of coder bros through his fabulous scrim of art film wooziness. I ask Garfield, now a two-time vet of the director’s films, to sum up the full Guadagnino psychedelic experience.

“Humanity and bodies and interpersonal dynamics and relationship and sexuality, sensuality, Eros, love, the muck and the mire of being human, ambition, drive, greed, power, love, brotherhood, connection,” he says. Guadagnino’s movies are about “his curiosity and love for people: wanting to skin, flay, open up, crack the ribs, and show the insides of these human beings.”

To Garfield this is the key to understanding the director’s vision for Artificial. Robots didn’t build the robots that might destroy humanity: People did. And people still control them—for now.

Artificial inspires a lot of comparisons. Barbaro likens it to Invasion of the Body Snatchers; Garfield compares its climactic confrontation scene to West Side Story. Guadagnino, the actor says, gave another point of reference. Then he does a spot-on, peak-Sicilian impression of the director: “I want this to be like a John Hughes movie.”

Guadagnino himself is reluctant to name any films that may have inspired this one. But he does name one filmmaker—someone who, as he notes, balanced indie flicks with blockbusters all while building the world’s greatest collection of Haitian art: Jonathan Demme.

“Jonathan was a humanist, and he had this very profound capacity of eviscerating dynamics of humanism in America,” Guadagnino says. “He did some great movies about the dynamics of corporations versus individual freedom,” like Fighting Mad and Philadelphia.

Barbaro says the film’s secret sauce is that it’s up for interpretation. It’s possible to come away from it celebrating the AI bros as heroes or decrying them as villains.

“It’s a bit of a Rorschach test,” she says. “Some people come out shaking, terrified. And I think some people are like, ‘Wow, what a good time!’ I also think that you have to hide the medicine in the food a little bit. I don’t think a purely doomsday story is going to reach many people.”

UNDER PRESSURE “I felt very impressed that Amazon wanted to make the film,” Garfield says. “They didn’t kill it. They could have killed it.”

Garfield, meanwhile, may leave the film eternally bonded with Altman—the role that could help him finally clinch the Oscar. (Garfield’s been nominated twice but hasn’t won yet.) Before making Artificial, Garfield says, he had a positive impression of Altman. He seemed friendly, “like maybe we would’ve been buddies on the kibbutz.”

As he dove deeper, though, Garfield’s feelings about Altman got stranger and more complicated in ways that the film addresses both head-on and obliquely. Is Altman someone who habitually tells tall tales? Uses lies to say what needs to be said, as Sam tells Ilya in the movie? Imagines anecdotes about waving to the A-lister who’s playing him in a biopic?

Whatever Altman’s relationship with reality is, the version of him we see in Artificial is charming, ingratiating, prone to grandiose hallucinations and to telling people exactly what they want to hear—then doing what he was going to do anyway. He’s not far off from an AGI approaching a real human consciousness, art imitating a machine imitating life.

“There are certain threads that feel consistent, which is a questioning of his ability to tell or his commitment to the truth,” Garfield says. “How often is he telling the truth to himself? How often is he telling the truth to others? And how many versions of the truth are there, and how is he utilizing that in order to...”

“Because I ultimately do believe that Sam feels, in our film and in life, that he is serving the good of mankind.”

It’s beginning to look a lot like Snoggletog in the Isle of Berk.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The love, joy and merriment of the holiday season are always infectious in theme parks. As part of Universal Epic Universe’s holiday celebration expansion for 2026, the decorations have been scaled up (sorry, I had to work a dragon reference in there) in How to Train Your Dragon – Isle of Berk for Snoggletog, and guests are all the better for it.

I got to experience the newborn theme park’s first holiday season in 2025, which was festive but also promised so much future possibility. Seeing what Universal was able to pull together just six months into the opening of their newest theme park just made me want more of everything. At that time, Snoggletog was relegated to a banner hung in the Isle of Berk gift shop that you could miss and never know it was there if you didn’t wander inside. So, I was particularly excited to learn that this year, the annual holiday inspired by modern Christmas traditions would be expanded throughout the land.

For those not in the know, Snoggletog is the winter holiday celebrated by the Viking community on the fictional Isle of Berk in the How to Train Your Dragon franchise. It features feasts and festivities fit for dragons and even includes the seasonal Harvest Mac & Cheese Cone at Hooligan’s Grog & Gruel. And there’s now a row of trees, just inside the entrance, decorated with what looks to be homemade ornaments that are a fun detail to check out during the day and beautiful to look at once they’re lit up at night.

Epic Universe is already a big award winner and popular destination with a ton of great attractions. I appreciate that they’re not wasting any time by expanding their offerings, too, even with something that seems as small as holiday decorations. (Not to mention there’s that construction on an Epic Universe expansion for an indoor coaster.)

While my own gothic heart remains in Darkmoor, through the Dark Universe portal, Isle of Berk feels like the most expansive and detailed area of Epic Universe, so it’s especially nice to see this holiday celebration get the extra attention it deserves. It’s true, Toothless has yet to don a Santa hat, but you never know what could be added next year and into the future.

You can check out a video overview of Snoggletog during the daytime via Orlando Informer below:

A post shared by Orlando Informer (@orlandoinformer)

I have to say, the thing that most caught my eye was the wreath full of apples. It’s the perfect decor idea that not only looks beautifully festive but would also just be delicious. I also love that you can find a tree made of wood inside Hiccup’s Workshop that you could probably easily replicate if you’re crafty, or you can just pick up themed ornaments for your own home holiday tree.

If you’re going to be in Orlando in the near future, you can experience Snoggletog at Epic Universe and then head over to the Universal Orlando Resort, where you can have a very merry Grinchmas while also rounding out your theme park trip with what is the best theme park holiday parade through January 3, 2027.

#3645. Apple Podcasts 2026 Show of the Year is ‘Baby, this is Keke Palmer’

Each year, Apple Podcasts names its Show of the Year, and the 2026 winner is Baby, this is Keke Palmer. Apple said the podcast consistently ranked as one of the most popular shows, and praised it for its “exceptional quality and cultural impact” …

For anyone unfamiliar, the show is an interview format, but aims to dig a little deeper than most.

Palmer invites some of the biggest names in entertainment and culture to share the experiences that have shaped them. From exploring self-worth with Oprah Winfrey to discussing creativity, reinvention, and fatherhood with Anderson .Paak, she moves effortlessly between laugh-out-loud exchanges and thoughtful reflections on life, relationships, and success […]

The show pairs Palmer’s quick wit with genuine curiosity, striking a balance between humor and thoughtful inquiry that makes even the most recognizable guests feel like close friends. Her natural ability to connect with people draws audiences into every conversation, while her candor and energy bring a refreshing and unique authenticity to the interview format.

Palmer said that authenticity was a key goal for the show, both for herself and for her guests, and she encourages other creators to take the same path.

Don’t try to manufacture a personality for the camera. Develop a relationship with yourself, get comfortable expressing what is already there, and let the camera capture that […]

Preparation is supposed to support the conversation, not control it. I’m always listening for that moment when somebody says something that opens up an entirely new question.

You can watch or listen to the show here.

#3644. The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Timeline Explained – When Does It Take Place?

Don't train for the Hunger Games if you haven't seen "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" or the original set of "Hunger Games" films — spoilers ahead!

Suzanne Collins, the author of the "Hunger Games" books, doesn't reliably write new stories set within this expansive, totalitarian universe. 10 years after the final novel in her original trilogy, "Mockingjay," hit shelves, she decided to write "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," a prequel that brings us back to some of Panem's earliest days. Similarly, her 2025 book "Sunrise on the Reaping" looks at the 50th Hunger Games.

So, how does the "Hunger Games" timeline even work at this point? It's actually still pretty streamlined, even with Collins jumping around in said timeline across various books. With that in mind, let me walk you through it.

We'll return to "Ballad" and the original trilogy in a moment (all of which have blockbuster movie adaptations, obviously), but as for "Sunrise on the Reaping," the film version stars Joseph Zada as young Hunger Games victor Haymitch Abernathy and sits smack in the middle between "Ballad" and the very first "Hunger Games" book and movie. During the 50th Games (which, as the second "Quarter Quell" — meaning, an extra-evil edition of the Games held every 25 years — features 48 teenage tributes fighting to the death on TV instead of 24), Haymitch makes important alliances, defies the odds, and emerges as the winner. Decades later, he serves as a mentor to characters we meet in "The Hunger Games," making "Sunrise on the Reaping" an important bridge between "Ballad" and the other "Hunger Games" stories.

(A note: specific years are never mentioned in the franchise, so we just use iterations of the Games to organize its timeline.)

In 2020, Suzanne Collins released "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" (her first "Hunger Games" book in a decade), and it focused on the 10th Hunger Games and a young Coriolanus Snow, the man who grows up to be the oppressive president of the totalitarian dystopia known as Panem. In both the book and its film adaptation (where Coriolanus, or "Coryo," is played by Tom Blyth), we meet Coryo as his family faces poverty, total reputational ruin, and even eviction from their home in the Capitol. Desperate to claw his way back up the ladder (his family has a saying that "snow lands on top"), Coryo decides that the tribute he mentors must win the 10th Games, which are newly televised and which take place in a downtrodden, themeless arena (something that changes quite a bit as the Games continue).

Unfortunately for Coryo, his dean at the Capitol Academy, Casca Highbottom (Peter Dinklage), hated Coryo's deceased dad and gives him a tribute from the impoverished coal mining district, 12, assuming she can't possibly win. That, admittedly, backfires: Songstress Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler) from the musical Covey not only charms viewers watching the Games at home, but Coryo himself, and he helps her cheat and win the Games.

When Coryo's machinations are discovered, he's sent to become a Peacekeeper in District 12 ... and despite reuniting with Lucy Gray there, he keeps secrets that send her fleeing, and his descent into depravity truly begins. We do see Snow in "Sunrise on the Reaping" (as president and played by Ralph Fiennes in the movie adaptation), and appropriately, he warns Haymitch about girls from the Covey after learning about his Covey girlfriend and Lucy Gray's descendant, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak).

President Snow is still Panem's leader by the time we get to "The Hunger Games" and are introduced to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), the girl and boy chosen to represent District 12 in the 74th annual Hunger Games. Haymitch, portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the original films, is their mentor, and he initially phones it in after years of mentoring young tributes only to watch them die on TV in variously horrifying ways. He does take a shine to Katniss, though, identifying with her stubborn nature and unwillingness to listen to figures of authority, and before long, the two are essentially working together to try and protect the genuinely kind and good-hearted Peeta.

When Katniss and Peeta are allowed to jointly win the 74th Games, Snow wants revenge after a teenage girl makes him look like a fool. As a result, the Third Quarter Quell, the 75th Games, only pulls existing victors back into the arena ... and Peeta volunteers when Haymitch's name is called, sending him and Katniss back into the arena just a year after their win. These Games end abruptly, however, when Katniss fires an arrow through the force field surrounding the arena. She and Haymitch then decamp to the rebellious District 13, while Peeta is captured.

Eventually, the rebellion succeeds, Snow is defeated, and Katniss, Peeta, and Haymitch live out the rest of their lives in District 12. Hence, "Sunrise on the Reaping" fits perfectly into the existing "Hunger Games" movie timeline (it marries "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" and the stories that kicked off the Hunger Games franchise), and it's in theaters starting tonight.

Universal Epic Universe is currently celebrating its second holiday season with more holiday decorations than last year and a new Dark Universe ride currently under construction. There’s even more gifts from the theme park during this time of merriment! It’s just been announced that for the first time ever Epic is going to be added into the Annual Pass mix. The news led to a mix of huge excitement and tons of questions.

In a Universal Parks announcement, the Orlando resort shared that annual passes featuring Universal Epic Universe access are coming in early December. Guests with current annual passes will be able to upgrade their current passes, and those looking to purchase one can do so at this time. Unlike the other parks, there will be a reservation system in place with the earliest date to go with a pass being January 4, 2027. Check out some of the spirited reactions from Twitter:

Ever since Epic Universe opened its gates in May of last year, it has quickly become a favorite park with tons of great rides to check out. For those who want to return there again and again (and perhaps make time to notice the park’s fun easter eggs) an annual pass is always a great value. Fans are rightfully hyped.

Whenever there’s a big change at one of Universal Orlando’s parks, inquiries typically follow, and there’s a lot popping up amidst the announcement. Here’s a few big ones:

Universal was all over the comment section trying to answer some of these questions. Most of them seem to point to there being another wave of details on the way, but for now Universal Orlando’s Annual Pass website has been refreshed with current steps to take if you'd like to upgrade.

Universal Orlando Resort will still offer four different types of pass tiers, but the announcement includes a complete re-branding of the system. Those who hold these memberships will be called “Pass Members” rather than “Passholders” and the type names will go from being called Seasonal, Power, Preferred and Premier to Bronze, Silver, Gold and Platinum. They’re also going completely digital with all physical passes being phased out over time.

In regards to the Epic Universe upgrade, current Passholders will be given a timeframe for when they can upgrade their passes, and current holders will be able to switch before anyone else. Those who are in their renewal period will also have the option to “pay a price difference of $125 to $410 to renew into a Pass with Universal Epic Universe access, depending on Pass type.” Annual passes currently cost between $475 and $1015, based on that price difference info; the price range might have changed to between $600 to $1425, but all the details are not yet clear to anyone quite yet.

Universal is already teasing more information on the way “soon." Either way, it’s quite exciting that those interested will soon get to enjoy Epic Universe over and over.

#3641. Face unlock is a good compromise for the iPhone Duo – now let’s have it for the Mac

When Apple first announced Face ID, the company talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.

Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security …

The first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011. This didn’t include any extra hardware, simply using the front-facing camera to take a photo and compare this to a stored image of the user.

It took just days to discover just how insecure this approach is, with unlock achieved simply by holding up a photo of the owner’s face on another device. Yet even as late as 2019, Samsung was continuing to use this approach.

Meantime, in 2017 Apple launched Face ID in the iPhone X. This has an entire hardware module devoted to it, with infrared emitters and receivers used to create a 3D map of the shape of our face. This cannot be fooled by photos or even models, and Apple said at the time there was a less than a one in a million chance of it being fooled (with riders for twins, etc).

Face ID projects more than 30,000 invisible IR dots. The IR image and dot pattern are pushed through neural networks to create a mathematical model of your face and send the data to the secure enclave to confirm a match, while adapting to physical changes in appearance over time. All saved facial information is protected by the secure enclave to keep data extremely secure, while all of the processing is done on-device […] The probability that a random person in the population could look at your iPhone or iPad Pro and unlock it using Face ID is less than 1 in 1,000,000.

Given the massive contrast in security of the two approaches, it might seem odd that Apple is now adapting a purely visual face unlock feature. The only reason the company is doing this is because the lack of Face ID has been far and away one of the biggest complaints about the iPhone Duo.

I suspect Apple made the decision reluctantly and over the protests of security engineers. But while face unlock remains a very insecure approach compared to Face ID, Apple’s approach tries to strike a good balance between convenience and security. The following safeguards apply:

That latter restriction means it can’t be used for Apple Pay, to unlock password-protected apps, to open the Passwords app, or to do anything else that requires authentication – such as changing your passcode or adding a fingerprint to Touch ID.

I do not see any downside provided the feature is off by default and only those who want it will turn it on. Presumably with an explanation of the reasons it gives reduced security.

For myself, I have got so used to using touch ID on my keyboard that I'd likely not make use of it in my business. If anything goes wrong with client information, I want to know, and be able to demonstrate, that I have taken security seriously.

There’s only one other safeguard I’d like to see Apple introduce: geolocking. Personally, I’d want to be able to allow face unlock at home, but disable it when I’m out and about. Currently, the only two ways to temporarily disable it are to toggle it off or to restart the phone. I’d like to see an option to set safe locations, like home and work, with the feature disabled in public.

Given that Face unlock requires only a front-facing camera, there’s absolutely no reason why Apple couldn’t also make it available on the Mac.

Face ID has been something MacBook users have been wanting for a great many years, and despite a decade’s worth of Apple patents for just this, it still hasn’t happened. Face unlock would be a compromise option that would at least get us some of the way there. I see I’m not the first to suggest this, with Macworld’s Roman Loyola beating me to it.

What’s your view? If you own an iPhone Duo, will you choose to enable this? If you own a MacBook, would you like the same option on that? Please take our poll and share your thoughts in the comments.

#3640. Dolly Parton on Her Mother Avie Lee Parton’s Album, Mama Sings

Many people know of my mama, Avie Lee Owens Parton, from my song “Coat of Many Colors,” but my mama gave me a gift that was far more valuable than a colorful coat. She gave me the gift of music.

As far back as I can remember, Mama loved to sing—at church, at family get-togethers, and most of all to her children. Her love of music came naturally; she had inherited it from her parents, her grandparents, and all the way back to Wales, where her family, the Owens, came from. Most of all, she inherited her love of music from her father, the Rev. Jake Owens. Grandpa Owens was a singer, songwriter, musician, and music teacher, in addition to being a full time Pentecostal preacher. He and my grandma Rena raised eight children, and all of them took to music in one way or another.

So, it was a natural thing that Mama shared her love of music with her children. She especially loved the old mountain songs—ballads that reached all the way back to the British Isles, popular songs from the 1800s that mountain people had made their own and, of course, beloved hymns.

So, when my uncle Louis Owens, Porter Wagoner, and I opened Fireside Recording Studio in Nashville in 1973, both my uncle Louis and I knew we had to get Mama in the recording studio to capture her songs on tape. Working with just a guitarist and an autoharp player, Mama recorded her own versions of some of her favorite songs.

Dolly Parton, Carl Butler, Avie Lee Parton, Robert Lee Parton, and Pearl Butler.

The plan was to release an album, but for one reason or another, it never happened. Fortunately, my uncle Louis saved all the tapes, and when he passed away, his son Richie, who has always loved our family history and heritage, decided to clean them up and get them released.

Dolly Parton and her mother, Avie Lee Parton.

Many of them are well-known tunes, but you may know them under different titles. Like all mountain singers, Mama preferred to call songs by the name she’d learned them under, and we decided that that was the way we needed to present them to you.

If you’ve ever wondered where my music came from, this album tells the story, and I am so proud, happy, and honored to have shared this music and my mama’s voice with you.

#3639. Yellowjackets Season 4 Review: The Survival Thriller's Final Episodes Answer A Big Question

"What are we capable of when our darkest urges are given not only a voice, but also a stage on which to use it? And can you ever really go back once you've seen what's underneath?" asked Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson in the pitch deck for their thriller series "Yellowjackets," claiming this would be the central question driving their show. As "Yellowjackets" debuts its fourth and final season, its answer comes due.

Set in both the late 1990s and early 2020s, "Yellowjackets" follows the aftermath of a plane crash that was taking the Wiskayok, New Jersey Yellowjackets soccer team across the country to a national championship. The teenage survivors descend into a barbarity, cannibalism, and pagan ritual across 19 months stranded in the Canadian wilderness. In their present, their now middle-aged selves reckon with old wounds coming unsealed.

"Yellowjackets" returns from a third season that hit some stumbling blocks. The departure of Juliette Lewis in particular was a hard void to fill, even if the show is trying with the introduction of Hilary Swank as an adult counterpart to Yellowjacket Melissa (Jenna Burgess). But the season ended on a high note.

In the Season 3 finale, "Full Circle," Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) uses a salvaged satellite phone to call for rescue. With help's imminent arrival in the Wilderness, the Yellowjackets must scramble to tie up loose ends. In the present, Taissa (Tawny Cypress) and Misty (Christina Ricci), fed up with cleaning Shauna's (Melanie Lynskey) messes, are planning to kill her — until Melissa puts the spotlight on the Yellowjackets again.

Paramount+ has only shared the first two (out of ten) episodes of "Yellowjackets" Season 4 for review. Going off that extremely limited view of the season, the ride is steady enough so far.

It's been a nail-biting wait for the return of "Yellowjackets," especially knowing since last October this would be the end of the show. I'll admit I've been counting down the weeks for Season 4, yet when I first received those screeners, I held off for several days. Suddenly the reality of the show ending, and the risk of it disappointing, became too real.

As previously confirmed by the creators, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 is the most structurally complex season yet. Now there are three parallel timelines, as we see play out in these first two episodes. The adult Yellowjackets are still in one story, but the teens are in two. Instead of depicting their rescue and readjustment in chronological order, Season 4 cuts back and forth between their last days in the wilderness and their first days back in Wiskoyak. Taissa (Jasmin Savoy Brown) is taking lead as the one keeping the other Yellowjackets on script — she does grow up to be a lawyer and politician, after all.

Knowing "Yellowjackets" was originally planned for five seasons, it's tempting to consider if this new structure is a way to cram the remainder of the 1990s timeline into one densely-packed season. Indeed, we see very little of the Wilderness timeline in these first two episodes, which will frustrate some since that's still the most exciting storyline. It's got the running clock, as the Yellowjackets have to get their stories and evidence straight without knowing exactly when help is arriving, and the biggest mysteries, since we know that a few more of the Yellowjackets are going to die in the time gap.

"Yellowjackets" Season 3 previously skipped months ahead of Season 2's cliffhanger ending. Watching the Season 4 premiere, with the Yellowjackets recuperating in a hospital, you might think the show has done so again. After all, Season 3 ended with Nat calling for help, so it's not a huge jump. Plus, is there any more story to tell in the Wilderness? Indeed there is, because the last minutes cut back and forth to violence still unseen. But is it wise to fall back on the "keep the audience waiting" trick in your last season?

Opening on the immediate post-rescue timeline, though, delivers on a promise the show has made since the beginning. Since we've known from the jump that some of the team makes it home, the show invites you to imagine what will happen when that moment arrives. How will they adjust to seeing their old parents and peers again, who have no idea what their daughters and friends faced for 19 months? The Season 4 premiere finally introduces many of the characters' parents, and sets up a season exploring the Yellowjackets' home lives, like what made them into the people they were before the Wilderness.

How does the 1990s timeline bridge to the 2020s one? How do the Yellowjackets assimilate to suburban mundanity? How will they handle the unwanted public spotlight that flattens them into sainted heroes but also piles on the salacious theories of what they did to survive? How do they cover up any and all investigations into their crimes that still remain buried as of 2022? "Yellowjackets" Season 4 is on track to deliver all those answers and, so far, they appear promising.

As for the 2020s timeline, the premiere picks up with Melissa, catching up to where she went after running off in Season 3 Episode 9 "How The Story Ends." The show still hasn't quite overcome what a narrative patch her introduction was back in Season 3. Now, though, she is at least giving the present day timeline a villain and conflict uniting the other Yellowjackets, something the show has struggled with after Season 1.

The adult timeline of "Yellowjackets" is often best when the leads are together. In Season 4, they're sharing a united front early on instead of converging mid-season. Let's also just say that how Melissa re-inserts herself into her old friends' lives fits the absurdist black comedy the show excels at, and it's looking like it could be an impetus for the Yellowjackets to finally earn a public reckoning.

Conversely, the teen timeline looks like it might be splitting the girls up as they slot back into their old, separate lives without the Wilderness binding them together. But the teen timeline actors, who've always held the show up through peaks and valleys, remain as strong as ever.

Shauna's (Sophie Nélisse) brief reign as the Wilderness' cannibal Antler Queen is over, and she's not happy about it. She says very little as her anger stews; she's cowed and quiet, but not regretful. Episode 2 focuses mostly on Shauna, and the very beginning of how she's going to force herself into a box of domestic tranquility for two decades — a box that her middle-aged self is breaking out of.  Shauna's mask is off again and it's scary, and also incredible how Melanie Lynskey makes her sweet, high-pitched voice sound as cold and sharp as an icicle.

The show's usual MVPs remain Sophie Thatcher in the teen timeline — Natalie is the one Yellowjacket not returning to a happy home — and Christina Ricci in the adult timeline. Misty's manically planning to stage Shauna's suicide brings out her unhinged comic relief side; no one can do a wide-eyed, violent smile like Ricci.

Yet, dialogue is a mixed bag. There's plenty of clever and cutting lines, but a bit too much hand-holding exposition recaps, as well. The killer soundtrack of "Yellowjackets," though, remains on point, bringing out '90s favorites like Nirvana and Depeche Mode for montage sequences. The most striking needle drop is in Episode 2, when Shauna is walking alone at night (a genuinely eerie shot) to Portishead's "Wandering Star."

Blunt yet clever visual storytelling is on the menu in these episodes, too. Take Lottie (Courtney Eaton) sitting in a hospital exam room where the wall is painted with a forest full of Disney-like animals, a reminder of her abandoned Wilderness home. Continuing on from a dream sequence in Season 3 Episode 8's "A Normal Boring Life," Season 4 Episode 2 uses a grocery store as the ultimate setting of modern normality (the contrast, of course, is that the Yellowjackets had to fight and scavenge for their food in the Wilderness).

Shauna is surrounded by seemingly innocuous reminders of her last 19 months as the group's butcher (in more ways than one), like sliced deli meat or a dead deer (crowned with antlers) being sliced up as roadkill. If this season can stick the landing, the legacy of "Yellowjackets" should be stronger than Shauna's as the Antler Queen.

"Yellowjackets" Season 4 premieres on Paramount+ on Friday, November 20, 2026.
