#3609. How to hide the new macOS 27.3 menu bar indicator

macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another.

If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround.

I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.

Open Terminal and run these two commands:

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domainsudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false

Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac.

The command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator.

To restore Apple’s default behavior, run:

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR

Restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured.

This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future update.

#3608. 32 Years Later, Mufasa's Best Lion King Line Is Still The Greatest Disney Quote Ever

"The Lion King" is the crowning achievement of the Disney Renaissance. If you were born after, say, 1989, then the movie was almost certainly a cornerstone of your childhood. That makes it amusing to look back and realize Disney didn't expect "The Lion King" to be one of the studio's greatest works.

Directed by Roger Allers and Rob Minkoff, "Lion King" was the highest grossing film of 1994 and, at the time, the second highest grossing film in history (earning more than $770 million during its initial release). More than any other animated Disney classic, "The Lion King" is a franchise unto itself — it's even been adapted as a Broadway play.

The 1998 sequel, "The Lion King II: Simba's Pride," is pretty good as far as direct-to-video Disney sequels go. Scene-stealing comic relief, and Simba's foster fathers, Timon & Pumbaa (Nathan Lane & Ernie Sabella, whose audition changed the movie), got their own TV show and spin-off movie "The Lion King 1 ½." Disney Jr. aired a sequel TV series, "The Lion Guard," and in 2019, Disney produced a photorealistic "Lion King" remake that got its own prequel, "Mufasa." Granted, that remake only proved how special the original and its luscious cartooning is.

An essential part of the majesty of "The Lion King" is the movie's sound. Hans Zimmer's Oscar-winning score, plus songs composed by Elton John with lyrics by Tim Rice. Even if you don't speak the Zulu language, who can't recall the opening "Circle of Life" song as all of the savannah marches to pride rock to pay tribute to new prince Simba (Jonathan Taylor Thomas)? Then there's the voice acting, especially the late James Earl Jones as Simba's father Mufasa — no voice in cinema history better feels like a real father and a king all at once.

Mufasa is murdered early on in "The Lion King" by his envious brother Scar (Jeremy Irons) staging a wildebeest stampede to trap Simba. (This complex sequence took three years to animate properly.) Simba, convinced by Scar it's all his fault, runs away in shame and spends years living in exile, learning "Hakuna Matata" (It means no worries!) from Timon and Pumbaa. When his childhood friend Nala (Moira Kelly) comes knocking, the grown Simba (Matthew Broderick) has to finally face his past.

With help from mandrill shaman Rafiki (Robert Guillaume), that's what Simba does. Mufasa once told Simba to look up into the sky to remember his father would always be with him. Mufasa literally manifests in the clouds, pushing Simba to fulfill his birthright: "Remember who you are. You are my son and the one true king."

"The Lion King" is often called a kid-friendly staging of "Hamlet" with talking animals. This scene mirrors the ghost of Hamlet's murdered father talking to his son. But James Earl Jones' voice is so grand that it feels more like God speaking to Christ.

Yet the scene also unfurls common criticism of "The Lion King" for its themes and political subtext. Textually, "The Lion King" is a pro-monarchy movie. It is quite literally about how the restoration of the proper heir to the throne heals the world. (The movie stacks the deck by making Scar a lazy and ill-equipped king on top of him being a kinslayer.) Mufasa frames Simba as the rightful king simply because he's the son of a king, suggesting (to quote Princess Azula of "Avatar: The Last Airbender") that "the divine right to rule is something you're born with." Pretty regressive attitude for the 1990s, but it's undeniably epic storytelling, too.

"The Lion King" is filled with memorable quotes and song lyrics from its ensemble, so let's narrow that and list only Mufasa's greatest lines. Besides the inimitable power of James Earl Jones' voice, Mufasa's limited screentime — most of it spent schooling or bond with his son — makes every bit of his dialogue feels special.

#3606. We Officially Ranked Every Season of 'The Sopranos'

The Sopranos is hailed as one of the greatest television shows of all time, known for its impeccable writing, unexpected depth, and unforgettable performances. Created by David Chase, the series follows James Gandolfini as Tony Soprano, a New Jersey mob boss who seeks help from a psychiatrist (Lorraine Bracco) for panic attacks, turning him into a mirror for the audience’s own appetite for violence, loyalty, and self-delusion. Ranking its seasons is a strange, almost unfair exercise because its weakest stretches contain scenes most dramas would kill for: a family dinner gone sour, a dream sequence that unravels a man’s whole life, a road trip to college that turns into a murder. But the seasons are not interchangeable.

Some are tight, propulsive machines built around a single threat while others sprawl, drift, and gamble on tone, and a few of those gambles are the reason people are still arguing about this show decades later. For this ranking, I weighed a few things: how well each season stands on its own as a story, how it deepens Tony and the people orbiting him, the strength of its standout episodes, and how boldly it takes creative risks. Fair warning: the hardest part wasn’t deciding what belongs at the top. It was deciding which brilliant season has to sit at the bottom.

Season six lands at the bottom, and it’s less a failure than a victim of impossible standards. Split awkwardly into two parts across more than a year, it never builds the momentum of the tighter seasons before it. Part one is strong, but the season as a whole feels like a show running out of road and losing its focus. Vito Spatafore’s (Joseph R. Gannascoli) storyline, though ambitious, takes up enormous space and ends up feeling disconnected from the rest of the show. A. J. Soprano's (Robert Iler) depression arc is thematically rich, but it often plays out as grim rather than revealing.

Another major issue is the overall pacing. Several episodes drift without urgency, and the final nine feel more like a series of elegant gestures than a driving story. Tony’s near-death experience in Atlantic City promises a transformation, but the show quietly retreats from it, leaving his growth stalled. Even the much-debated finale, brilliant as it is, rewards viewers for admiring its ambiguity rather than its payoff and is widely cited as HBO's most controversial ending. Season six has some of the series’ sharpest moments, but when compared with the tension of season one or the tragedy of season five, it simply has less to hold together. Even a weaker season of The Sopranos is better than most shows’ best, but someone has to finish last.

The show's fifth season sits second to last not because it lacks greatness, but because it’s the season most dependent on a single, familiar idea. The season premieres with the return of Tony Soprano’s cousin Tony Blundetto (Steve Buscemi), who is fresh out of prison and determined to go straight, setting up a tragedy that’s easy to see coming. Once he slides back into his former life, the season spends too many episodes waiting for the inevitable. That predictability matters. Earlier seasons kept viewers off balance, but here the central conflict feels more like a slow march than a surprise. Blundetto is compelling, yet he’s also a rerun of the show’s oldest theme: you can’t escape who you are.

The Johnny Sack (Vincent Curatola) and New York storyline adds menace, but it often runs parallel to the main plot rather than driving it. Meanwhile, Carmela’s (Edie Falco) arc, including her entanglement with Furio’s (Federico Castelluccio) absence and her growing resentment, is abundant but occasionally sidelined by the larger crime story. Season five also benefits from its place in the series, which makes its relative weakness feel harsher. Coming after the lean tension of the early years and before the bold stretch to the finish line, it can read as a holding pattern, but episodes such as 'Irregular Around the Margins' and 'The Strong, Silent Type' remain stunning hours of small-screen entertainment.

Season four earns its ranking because it’s the show at its most diffuse. Where earlier seasons organized themselves around a clear antagonist, the fourth season spreads across a looser collection of threads, and the result feels more like a series of vignettes than a single driving story. The central tension, Tony’s feud with Carmine Lupertazzi (Tony Lip) and the New York family over the Esplanade construction deal, simmers but rarely boils. Meanwhile, Ralph Cifaretto’s (Joe Pantoliano) rise and eventual downfall is gripping but resolves mid-season, leaving the back half searching for momentum.

There’s also a restlessness to the season’s mood that is impossible to ignore after a certain amount of time. Moments of deep tragedy, like Adriana La Cerva's (Drea de Matteo) gradual unraveling, share space with oddly broad humor, and the balance doesn’t always land.

Either way, the fourth season still contains episodes like 'Whoever Did This' and 'Whitecaps,' which are considered by many to be some of the most enthralling moments in modern television ever produced. This was a tough choice, but third from the bottom on a show this great is still a high-water mark for almost any other drama.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

Season one of The Sopranos takes the third spot because it’s the purest version of what the show set out to do. Thirteen episodes, one clear threat, and no wasted motion. Tony’s war with Uncle Junior (Dominic Chianese) gives the season a spine that later years, for all their ambition, sometimes lack. Every subplot feeds it, from Christopher Moltisanti (Michael Imperioli) and Brendan Filone’s (Anthony De Sando) reckless hijackings to Livia’s (Nancy Marchand) quiet scheming in the background. What lifts it above the weaker seasons is how fully formed the show’s voice already is.

The panic attacks, the therapy sessions with Dr. Melfi, and the tension between family and “the family” arrive with total confidence. Tony is introduced as a man in crisis, not a legend, and that vulnerability gives the violence weight. The season also contains some of the series’ defining hours, notably 'College,' which turns a routine road trip into a masterpiece of dread and marks a major turning point for Gandolfini's character, while 'Isabella' shows the show’s willingness to get strange almost immediately. It stops short of the top two because the stakes, while sharp, are narrower than what came after, but as a debut, it’s nearly flawless. There are very few shows that start this strong, and there are even fewer that still hold up this well on a rewatch.

Season three lands as the show's second runner-up because it may be the series at its most confident, funny, and unsettling all at once. It’s the season where The Sopranos stops proving it can do everything and simply does it. The introduction of Joe Pantoliano's arrival as Ralph Cifaretto gives the season a genuinely terrifying presence as he conveys his character as charming, petty, and capable of sudden cruelty, making it clear that the show has no intention of letting viewers off the hook. Ralph’s volatility pushes Tony into some of his most compromised choices, and his conflict with Tony sharpens the season’s moral stakes.

Meanwhile, the Jackie Aprile Jr. (Jason Cerbone) storyline is a quiet tragedy about inheritance, and Meadow’s (Jamie Lynn-Sigler) role in it adds real emotional cost. Carmela’s arc is richer too, as her loyalty to Tony and her need for something more real pull at her throughout. The season also balances its tone beautifully. Episodes such as 'Employee of the Month' and 'Pine Barrens' show how comfortably the writers could swing between brutality and absurdity, often in the same hour. Dr. Melfi’s storyline gives the season its dramatic center, and the gap between Tony’s therapy and his actions has never been starker. It narrowly misses the top spot only because season two builds a more complete, devastating arc, but season three is the show at full power.

Season two takes the top spot because it’s where The Sopranos achieves total control and essentially establishes its intentions. Every thread pulls toward the same devastating destination, and nothing feels wasted. The season’s backbone is Big Pussy’s (Vincent Pastore) betrayal, which is a constant source of intensity and uncertainty for fans. Once Tony learns his oldest friend has been wearing a wire, the show builds an agonizing slow burn, and “Funhouse” delivers its payoff as a feverish dream sequence that ranks among the greatest episodes in television history. Tony must kill a man he loves, and the show makes us feel every ounce of that cost.

Around that core, the season layers in Richie Aprile’s (David Proval) volatile return from prison, whose clash with Janice (Aida Turturro) produces both dark comedy and genuine shock. Livia’s death-haunted presence and Junior’s legal troubles keep the family tangled in old grievances, while Christopher’s rise and Adriana’s growing importance give the younger generation real weight. Season two also deepens the show’s central question: can Tony change? His therapy with Dr. Melfi grows more revealing, and “Full Leather Jacket” and “Bust Out” show the cost of the life he has chosen with remarkable economy. It outranks the others because it combines season one’s tight focus with season three’s confidence and adds an emotional gut punch the rest can’t quite match. Season two is not just the best of The Sopranos; it’s a master class in serialized storytelling.

#3605. iOS 27.3 will give iCloud+ subscribers two new perks

When iOS 27.3 beta 2 debuted earlier this week, we detailed how the update introduces AI usage limits for Siri AI and select other features.

For AI features that depend on server-based models, each device running iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, or macOS 27.3 will have limited daily access to advanced AI features. These include complex Siri AI requests, Image Playground, certain Photos app editing tools, and more.

The only iCloud+ tier that doesn’t include higher limits is the $0.99/month plan.

Read more: Apple reveals how iCloud+ increases Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage limits

In the Shortcuts app, the ‘Use Model’ action lets you choose between a few different model options, including Cloud, Cloud Pro, On-Device, and ChatGPT.

People should at least have the 200 GB model. When I worked at The Apple Store (Did Retail and Corporate) I always recommended iCloud, and highlighted the backup feature. I can’t tell you the amount of people who lost or got their phones damaged / destroyed and lost precious photos, videos that they could never get back. Nearly all signed up.

I did offer alternatives like backing to your Mac or external SSD, but to have a proper backup safety system you need 1-2 backups at home and one off site (ie. friends house, storage facility, etc.) and you would have to be consistent with your backups and drop offs. Most people don’t have the time so they do iCloud, same as I.

I’m at 2 TB, probably going to 6 TB, cause I love taking photos and videos of special events.

Similar to Apple’s other AI usage limits, your access to the Cloud Pro model in Shortcuts increases if you have a higher storage plan. Per this support document, the 200GB plan supports standard limits, the 2TB plan offers 5x access, followed by 10x on the 6TB plan and 20x on the 12TB plan.

iCloud+ already provided far more than just increased cloud storage, but with iOS 27.3 it’s set to be an asset for AI power users too.

iCloud+ is available as a standalone subscription or through the Apple One bundle, which also includes Apple TV, Apple Music, and more.

#3604. Yellowjackets Season 4 Premiere Adds One Of The Show's Biggest Missing Characters

This article contains spoilers for "Yellowjackets" Season 4 Episode 1 "Hivemind."

The "Yellowjackets" Season 4 marketing campaign has leaned hard on Alanis Morissette's song "Ironic," featuring it in both trailers for the season. A bunch of teenagers stuck in the wilderness for months are finally rescued, but they're all unhappy to be going home for one reason or another? Yeah, that's about as ironic as rain on your wedding day.

The fourth and final season has debuted (read /Film's review here) and it jumps ahead from Season 3's cliffhanger ending when Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) got an SOS call out of the Wilderness. In "Hivemind," the survivors are recovering in a Canadian hospital and, about halfway through the episode, they reunite with their parents. This introduces us to Shauna's (Sophie Nélisse) mother (Gabrielle Miller, who definitely looks convincing as the mother of a woman who grows up to be Melanie Lynskey).

Besides her parents being divorced, "Yellowjackets" has given us precious little information about Shauna's childhood home life. The first stretch of Season 1 episodes offered glimpses into some of the Yellowjackets' earlier childhoods, but not Shauna's. That has generated lots of "Fellowjacket" fan speculation, from fanfiction to forum posts, about what Shauna's mom is like. Shauna is the lead in the "Yellowjackets" ensemble, and her arc begins with her feeling invisible (including next to her best friend) before she becomes a tyrant in the Wilderness.

Information on Shauna's parents has felt like a missing piece to her character, especially since motherhood is also an essential theme for both iterations of Shauna. She was pregnant, from her future husband Jeff, while stuck in the Wilderness. In "Yellowjackets" Season 2, she suffered a stillbirth, during which she slipped into an extremely lucid dream of her teammates cannibalizing her newborn son.

The death of Shauna's baby shapes every part of her life afterward, from her desire to make everyone else miserable in the 1990s timeline to how, in the present day story, she keeps her daughter Callie (Sarah Desjardins) at arm's length. (Season 3 episode "Them's The Brakes" features teen Shauna experiencing a vision of her son still alive. Scored like "Rosemary's Baby," it's also the only time in Season 3 that Shauna looks truly happy.)

Now, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 can complete the puzzle by showing Shauna's relationship with her own mother. We don't get much of Mrs. Shipman in this episode, granted, but she seems naturally relieved to see her daughter is still alive. (That automatically makes her a better parent than Natalie's mom, who doesn't even bother to show up.) Shauna spends most of the episode silent and scowling. When doctors notice her medical exams suggest she's given birth recently, she clams up and denies it. Her mother notices Shauna was talking with an OB/GYN, though, and appears to put the pieces together.

"Hivemind" ends with the Yellowjackets and their parents on a plane back home to New Jersey, recreating a glimpse of their rescue seen in Season 2 premiere "Friends, Romans, Countrymen." At least some of the parents will be big supporting players this season; you don't do stunt casting like Molly Ringwald as Van's (Liv Hewson) mother if she was just (barely) going to be in this one episode. So, how will the Shipman household readjust now that Shauna's back? We'll find out, but that's not the only lingering question about Shauna.

When we last saw Shauna at the end of Season 3, she was freshly crowned as the Antler Queen. In "Hivemind," her face is horribly bruised and swollen. How'd that happen?

"Hivemind" might have you thinking the show is going to skip over the Yellowjackets' final days in the Wilderness. Instead, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 breaks down the show's fractured timeline even further, because the lead-up to the girls' rescue and their first days back home are being told in parallel. The very last scene of "Hivemind" features Natalie, having just made the SOS call, running back to the Yellowjackets' camp and exclaiming "what the f***?" at the sight waiting for her there, promising the show has more story to tell of the Wilderness.

At the very least, "Yellowjackets" Season 4 isn't repeating the major sin of Season 3. Season 2 ended with the Yellowjackets' cabin shelter burning down in the dead of winter. Then, Season 3 jumped over that cliffhanger months ahead to spring, where they'd already built new shelter and had pulled back on their descent into cannibalism and ritual. Just like that, the show skipped past the roughest stretch of the team's survival.

It was too big a jump. "Hivemind" — which pointedly features the survivors staying silent as they're grilled about what happened during their time stranded — delights in keeping the audience in suspense, almost like it wants you to think the show is again resolving a cliffhanger by leaping past it. Is holding out too clever by half? Or is this the most efficient way to keep the show's Wilderness thrills until the end while also delivering long-awaited stories like the Yellowjackets reuniting with their parents?

"Yellowjackets" Season 4 is streaming on Paramount+, with new episodes dropping on Fridays.

#3603. Persona 7 Already Teased Before Persona 6 Has an Official Release Date

The wait between Persona games won’t be as long in the future, Kazuhisa Wada promises

Now that Grand Theft Auto 6 is actually out and playable, we can no longer make "we really got X before GTA 6" jokes. Seemingly to make up for that loss, Atlus is giving us the opportunity to use the very same joke for Persona 6. The next mainline entry in the beloved RPG series was finally revealed this year, a decade after Persona 5 launched, but there is no sign of a release date. Even so, one Atlus producer is already giving fans hope for Persona 7.

In a Sega Sammy interview (as translated by GamesRadar+), P-Studio producer Kazuhisa Wada revealed that "Persona 6 is not the end. In order for Persona to grow as an IP, we consider how to live up to people's expectations in terms of creativity and development every day. Please look forward to more from the Persona series in the future."

Wada's comments don't explicitly reveal plans for Persona 7, but they do confirm Atlus is already thinking about what comes after Persona 6​​​​​​​. The producer also stated that the studio is working on shortening the time between releases. That could mean concurrent development or new tools to shorten the process, which Wada said takes at least five years. Alternatively, we could get more Persona spinoffs or remakes in the vein of the upcoming Persona 4 Revival. Footage of what appeared to be a remake of Persona 1 leaked earlier this month, though it still hasn't been verified.

Atlus revealed​​​​​​​ Persona 6 during a July Xbox showcase. The short teaser trailer was mostly vibes-based. It showed off a moody, green-hued graveyard, which suggests that the sixth mainline entry in the series could be returning to the darker, grittier tone of the franchise's early games.

Sega has confirmed that the game will get a physical edition on PlayStation 5 and Nintendo Switch 2. That suggests Persona 6 could be released prior to 2028, which is when Sony will stop producing new game discs. Sega and Atlus have suggested fans will hear more after Persona 4 Revival is released early next year.

#3601. The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Makes One Huge Change From The Book

Stop reading if the thought of kids fighting to the death in the arena makes your stomach turn — this article contains major spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping."

It's not a secret that, across the board, the Hunger Games franchise is dark and disturbing. Yet, the literary version of the 2025 prequel "Sunrise on the Reaping" somehow manages to make the books that came before it look like light-hearted fairytales, especially one plot point that may just be the most upsetting and depraved thing the Hunger Games property has ever done. Of course, in every literary and cinematic story set in this fictional universe, the titular games put actual children into dangerous arenas and force them to fight to the death, all while it's presented to the totalitarian regime of Panem and its captive citizens as televised entertainment. (Thankfully, the franchise does tend to center winners, so we don't have to watch all of our favorite characters killed in increasingly brutal ways.)

In the big screen adaptation of "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," every unsettling plot point appears in the movie, leading to some truly gutting moments as eventual victor Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) loses loved ones and allies. There's one notable difference from page to screen, though, and I can certainly understand why director Francis Lawrence made this tweak. The book is ... unrelentingly violent.

Again, some degree of violence is to be expected here if you consider the subject material, but "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" really dials back the gore. As an example, here are two gruesome moments depicted in the original book that aren't nearly as gross in the film adaptation of "Sunrise on the Reaping."

In both versions of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch and his fellow District 12 tributes, including Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), align themselves not with the super-charged Career tributes from wealthy districts but other underdogs, dubbing themselves "the Newcomers." One of those Newcomers is Ampert Latier (Percy Daggs IV), the son of former District 3 victor Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) who's only in the Games because the Capitol wants to punish Beetee for insubordination.

Ampert, Beetee, and Haymitch hatch a plan to smuggle an explosive into the arena and blow up a water tank that could flood the entire mechanism of the arena, and though Haymitch does set it off, the arena survives ... and the Gamemakers summarily punish him by killing Ampert with "muttations," or genetically engineered animals, in the form of squirrels. "I never even get a glimpse of Ampert, just writhing furry bodies fighting for a piece of him," Haymitch says in the book, and the movie does show this. It does not, however, show this:

"Panting, I watch them fade away. Then I turn back to what I am meant to witness. A small white skeleton, stripped clean to the bone. No flesh or clothing remains, only an ax at its right side, my knife at its left. My lips move, but no sound comes out. 'Buddy?' I stumble forward, spotting his tracker, wedged just below his elbow. There is no one to comfort, to ease out of this world. Ampert's been swallowed up by the Capitol, and his coffin will hold only these pearly white bones."

In the on-screen version, we simply see Ampert's body — not a clean skeleton.

Another newcomer that forms an alliance with Haymitch and Maysilee is Wellie, a diminutive District 6 tribute who's played in the film by Rada Rae. In the movie, as the tributes' numbers start to dwindle, Haymitch hears Wellie's token — a small bicycle bell — and is lured into a trap by Career tribute and formidable District 1 player Silka Sharp (Laura Marcus). The movie then skips ahead to that finale showdown between Silka and Haymitch, from which Haymitch emerges as the victor. The book is, again, far more explicit:

"Rounding a final clump of saplings, I freeze in horror at what awaits. Silka stands like a statue, her snot-green outfit splattered in bright red. In her right hand, her ax. Her left holds Wellie's head, eyes still open, mouth agape. The only movement, the only sound, comes from the blood dripping into the pine needles on the forest floor. Wellie's body lies crumpled in a heap a few feet away. The shiny silver bicycle bell. The blowgun. The child-sized boots. The tiny knife in her bird claw. Dove-colored feathers. Headless baby chick. I could live ten thousand years and never erase this sight from my memory."

It makes complete sense that the film version of "Sunrise on the Reaping" doesn't feature a kid's decapitated head — the movie is rated PG-13, after all. Still, if you haven't read "Sunrise on the Reaping," you should (it's really good!), and you should also know that it dials up the violence ante in a big way. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," which is overall extremely true to the book but scales back some of its most stomach-churning moments, is in theaters now.

#3600. Jensen Huang says he’s ready to rejoin Nvidia as CEO (if asked)

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

To be clear, I’m also willing to step in as CEO of Nvidia if asked. I’ve owned several generations of their graphics cards, so I have plenty of experience with their products. More importantly, this is probably my best chance of finally having enough cash to afford a Mac with 32GB of RAM.

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

Even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

Since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a new CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the company to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

#3599. 10 Classic Sci-Fi Shows That Are Better Than Modern Streaming Originals

There's nothing quite like the classics. As the streaming era has led television as a whole to evolve in ways nobody could have predicted a couple of decades ago, so too has small-screen science fiction transformed in several ways, leaving behind the days of classic sci-fi TV. But as powerful, high-quality, and undeniably cinematic as many sci-fi shows from the streaming era are, there are several classics which are simply unbeatable.

For the purposes of this list, any show that began before the advent of streaming in the 2010s, and which never became a streaming show (which discounts gems like Black Mirror and Futurama), will be considered a potential classic. However, age is only the first step. A true sci-fi classic is that which has had a great impact and influence on the genre, one so great and so pop-culturally relevant that it can be considered a must-see.

While working on the spy series Danger Man, Patrick McGoohan and George Markstein came up with the idea for The Prisoner. It's widely disputed whether McGoohan is the show's primary creator or the pair share true co-creator status, but one thing remains certain: This is one of those near-perfect sci-fi shows that nobody remembers anymore, a testament to the genius of British sci-fi storytelling.

Praised for its psychological depth, surreal brilliance, and avant-garde sensibilities, The Prisoner was absolutely revolutionary back in the '60s, pioneering auteur-driven television decades before it became the norm. It's both a deep countercultural allegory and one of the most entertaining sci-fi spy shows ever made, with a cryptic series finale that's among the most memorable in the genre's history.

After a brainstorming session at a Comic-Con while they were working on 2009's Star Trek, J. J. Abrams, Roberto Orci, and Alex Kurtzman came up with the idea for Fringe, one of the best spooky cop shows of all time. What started out as more of an episodic procedural inspired by the likes of The X-Files and The Twilight Zone soon turned into something far more serialized and creative.

The show knew exactly how to take full advantage of the constraints of network television in all the best ways, and it constantly demonstrated that mastery throughout its run. Instead of a regular "monster-of-the-week" procedural that might have gotten buried after a couple of seasons, Fringe proved that mysteries which seemed to be standalones could actually lay down the foundations for a much richer, more engaging multiverse.

After the success of Roland Emmerich's 1994 film Stargate, a franchise of the same title was launched forward, peaking just three years later. Indeed, Stargate SG-1 is not only the best installment in the whole franchise, but truly one of the greatest sci-fi shows of the network TV era. Spanning over 200 episodes, it took the film's high-concept premise and transformed it into a sprawling, timeless saga.

It's one of those sci-fi shows that shouldn't be remade, because how could you possibly top perfection? Stargate SG-1 still does everything right nearly two decades after its conclusion, from relying on a phenomenal cast playing some deeply engaging characters to a perfect blend between high-stakes drama and self-aware humor. The reason why it managed to run for a whopping 10 years is that it's among the most widely accessible sci-fi shows in history.

Cowboy Bebop is widely considered one of the biggest landmarks in the history of anime television, having fundamentally changed how global audiences and creators themselves viewed Japanese animation the world over. Never before had the world seen such a genre-bending and cinematic anime show, and rarely had the Western world fallen so deeply in love with a series like this.

It's one of the truest masterpieces of '90s anime television, a space Western with neo-noir tinges that's still just as stylish and universally entertaining today as it was decades ago. Generally considered one of the best gateway series for people who have never watched anime before, it's a visually stunning masterpiece with some of the best direction, writing, music, and voice acting that the medium has ever seen.

There are plenty of classic sci-fi shows that are better than most new series, and Babylon 5 is both one of the most noteworthy and one of the most massively influential. Quite unprecedented for American network television at the time, this space opera was written as a kind of novel for television, where each season was designed to serve as a new chapter in that story.

It's not like the small screen had never seen serialization before, but never before had sci-fi television seen serialization on this scale. Decades later, Babylon 5 still feels every bit as fresh and exciting as it did when it was originally on the air, and the technical elements that may look a bit dated only further add to its timeless charm. Without Babylon 5, sci-fi television as a whole wouldn't be what it is today.

There are plenty of sci-fi shows that have been canceled after only one short-lived season throughout the years, unable to reach their full potential — but none nearly as notorious or iconic as the space Western cult classic Firefly. It's one of the most perfect sci-fi shows of the last 25 years, one so great that one season was all it took for it to become one of the biggest sci-fi cult classics in the history of 21st-century television.

It was due to missteps unique to the network era of television, like airing episodes out of order, that Firefly didn't get to flourish, which only makes it even more of a crucial piece of network sci-fi television history. With its perfect blend of Americana aesthetics and fun sci-fi pulp, a delectably compelling ensemble of characters, and plenty of razor-sharp dialogue, it's no wonder why Firefly is as legendary as it is.

First airing in 1966, Star Trek: The Original Series proved that far from just being a source of pulpy entertainment, sci-fi could be a true mirror for contemporary social and political issues. Star Trek: The Next Generation grabbed that thematic thesis and carried it forward to lengths never seen before, delivering what many fans still agree is the best piece of Star Trek content to date.

With a top-tier cast led by the late Sir Patrick Stewart, some incredible production values, and some of the most profound and philosophically charged writing the genre has ever seen, The Next Generation is one of those space sci-fi shows that are genuine masterpieces. It's the space opera subgenre at its most optimistic and complex, and a must-see for anyone who even slightly enjoys network television sci-fi.

The original Battlestar Galactica from 1979 is still delightfully charming today, but it was seriously in need of an update. After several attempts to make either a sequel or a reboot, the series was finally born anew with the 2003 miniseries of the same name, which was followed by the full-length 2004 show that is nowadays remembered as one of the best sci-fi shows of the 21st century.

Indeed, Battlestar Galactica is one of those mega-addictive sci-fi shows that are impossible to stop watching, an absolutely legendary space opera that completely changed how broadcast science fiction looked, sounded, and felt. Rusty, gritty, and written as a thematic response to the national mood of the media following the 9/11 attacks, it's one of the most complex and well-written sci-fi shows of all time.

One of the most fun TV shows of the 1990s, The X-Files was a watershed moment in the history of broadcast television, pioneering the very concept of online fandom. To this day, its fans are still some of the most loyal and dedicated in the history of sci-fi television, and that's because this iconic show was so perfectly designed to endure the test of time.

Two FBI Special Agents solving mysteries together; one a fierce believer in the supernatural, the other a skeptic. It's a simple enough concept to base a sci-fi show on, but it's admirable just how long X-Files made that concept last. It's the gold standard for sci-fi procedurals, a real masterpiece of television's network era that always knew exactly how much serialization to inject into its episodic nature.

If there is any one show that deserves to be called the most influential in the history of sci-fi television, it's undoubtedly Rod Serling's The Twilight Zone, the greatest and most important anthology TV series of all time. Full of incredible stars, plenty of stellar writing, and some of the most genius high-concept premises in all of sci-fi television, it's a must-see classic without equal.

Like all anthology series, The Twilight Zone certainly had its highs and lows over the course of its run, but every single one of its seasons could reasonably be counted among the best anthology TV seasons of all time. It's the closest that sci-fi TV ever came to perfection throughout the entirety of the broadcasting era of the medium, and it will take something really special to ever top it during this new streaming era.

#3597. J.K. Rowling’s 6-Part Hit Crime Series Officially Confirms 2026 Release Date

The controversial author, Rowling, finally published Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone in 1997 after many rejections, and it led to it becoming the biggest book series in history. Since the seven novels concluded, the author has continued writing, whether that be to expand her Harry Potter universe, write other children's novels, write screenplays, or write under pseudonyms to venture into entirely new genres.

Rowling's new crime thriller adaptation is set to be released in one month, just weeks before the upcoming HBO Harry Potter series on December 6. Strike: The Running Grave will return for its seventh season, with Tom Burke back as Detective Cormoran Strike and Holliday Grainger as his partner, Robin Ellacott. It will adapt the seventh novel in Rowling's crime series, written under the pen name Robert Galbraith.

"When Sir Colin and Sally Edensor approach Cormoran Strike and Robin Ellacott, they are desperate to reconnect with their estranged son, Will. The Edensors enlist the detectives to gather evidence to discredit the Universal Humanitarian Church, a religious cult who have indoctrinated Will and siphoned off his trust fund."

The seasons include adaptations of The Cuckoo's Calling, The Silkworm, Career of Evil, Lethal White, Troubled Blood, The Ink Black Heart, and now, The Running Grave. The most recent installment of Strike, titled The Ink Black Heart, averaged over 7.1 million viewers, becoming the BBC's most-watched drama.

Burke and Grainger lead a guest cast including James Fleet (known for Bridgerton) as Sir Colin Edensor, Keeley Forsyth (known for Happy Valley) as Mazu Wace and Nichola McAuliffe (known for British soap opera EastEnders) as Shelley Heaton.

The British crime drama Strike first arrived in 2017, and it certainly had a strong reception within the UK before landing on HBO Max in 2021. Season 1, The Cuckoo's Calling, debuted to a strong critical reception and landed an impressive 85% on Rotten Tomatoes. Reviews stated, "It has style and good actors. These days, on television, much depends on the eye of the beholder, this is ever so true with the plot of this series," and "The seven hours are pleasingly old-school, too: no gratuitous violence, a lot of character development and the crimes wrap up like tidy parcels."

The news of Strike's return comes after the BBC announced a documentary exploring Rowling and her career, but also the controversial ideals she has been portraying across social media. At the time of writing, there is no official release date.

Fans of “The Gilded Age,” rejoice! There are still more luncheons to plan, more balls to savor, and more opera opening nights to fight over. Yes, the HBO original series has been renewed for a fifth season.

The move follows a surge in popularity that began with the show’s drama-filled third season, which saw Bertha (Carrie Coon) and George Russell’s (Morgan Spector) relationship strain, and has continued with the fourth season, which has dealt with their marriage troubles, the wedding of Peggy Scott (Denée Benton), and a visit from Grover Cleveland.

Related Stories Is A24 Finally Big Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio? Aaron Pierre on ‘Lanterns,’ the DC Shake-Up, and Landing a Role in Ryan Gosling’s ‘Star Wars’ Movie

The turnaround is striking because “The Gilded Age” was very much on the bubble for most of its first two seasons. Bringing 19th-century high-society to life is expensive, and the show initially struggled to become a ratings powerhouse despite being co-created by Julian Fellowes of “Downton Abbey” fame. In interviews, the cast admitted that they often feared they would be canceled. But audiences have shown up in a big way, and Fellowes and his co-creator Sonja Warfield recently told IndieWire that they have more stories to tell beyond this season.

“We have a Season 5 in us if we’re allowed to do it,” Fellowes said. “But when you write a TV series, you have to finish every season so that it could be the end, because one day it will be.”

In its three eligible seasons, “The Gilded Age” has earned 15 total Emmy nominations, including Outstanding Drama Series and Outstanding Directing for a Drama Series, as well as a Screen Actors Guild Award nomination for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series.

#3595. VSCO launches its first native Mac photo editor with RAW support, batch editing, more

VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the company’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside new features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the company’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the company’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing users to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

The first thing users will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

As for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the company’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for quickly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

And speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are new organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow users to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once users are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, users can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:

To learn more about VSCO Studio Pro Desktop, follow this link.

#3594. Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break

I don’t think I was supposed to hear Anthony Ippolito when he exclaimed, “20 minutes?” right before this interview, as he was given the amount of time this interview would last. Though, it kind of hit me, if you’re not used to doing interviews — and there’s no way Ippolito can be at this young stage of his career — 20 minutes is a long time to make conversation with a total stranger. Especially, as he is quick to point out, after a barrage of quick, three-minute interviews.

Ippolito has been in films and television before — kind of famously now, he played Al Pacino in “The Offer” — but none of those were roles in which he’d have to do press. Let alone playing the lead role in a major motion picture in which everyone wants to talk to him. Oh, and that lead role is as … Sylvester Stallone. Related Stories ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: David Fincher’s Breezy Tarantino Spinoff Is a Disappointing Compromise Between Great Directors Film Independent’s New President Wants to Build an L.A. Powerhouse — and Shake Up the Spirit Awards

In “I Play Rocky,” yes, Ippolito plays Stallone at the make or break point in Stallone’s career. Stallone had written “Rocky,” a very in-demand script. Not in demand was the idea of Stallone playing Rocky — as MGM offers more and more money to Stallone in an effort to get him to not play Rocky. (If you don’t know, Stallone stuck to his guns, played Rocky, and is now a very wealthy and famous actor.)

Directed by Peter Farrelly, Ippolito says he sent in multiple tapes trying to land this role — which does seem to be in the same spirit as the film itself. Though, Ippolito said, when he was actually going through the casting process, that’s not at all what he was thinking, even though it may seem that way now.

Ahead, he tells us (yes, over the course of 20 minutes) the Stallone movies he used to prep for playing Stallone, what is was like to talk to Stallone before filming, and why he loves Stallone and Dolly Parton together in “Rhinestone.” Also, if he had to play Stallone again in another movie, he does have another “I Play” installment in mind…

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: You seem excited about this being 20 minutes?

It’s a little strange, I’ve been having three-minute increment conversations with somebody. So, yes, I am excited.

OK, so how many Stallone movies did you watch? Did you stick to that era? His voice kind of evolves by the late ‘80s.

Yeah, I really tried to stay focused on a period of time. I don’t know the exact number. More so, from the stuff I was looking at I was watching it over and over again, rewatching. With the exception of a few.

Well, “Rocky Balboa.” It’s one of the best movies of the franchise.

For people who haven’t seen that one in a while, it’s very sweet.

It really is. It really is. And he does some excellent work in it. And I think it’s really powerful that he was able to come back many years later, after the fifth one, and make this incredible movie.

From closer to the “Rocky” era, I kind of love him in “The Prisoner of Second Avenue.” Jack Lemmon thinks he stole his wallet…

It’s just scene after scene of Jack Lemmon chasing Stallone through Central Park trying to get his wallet back…

But then Jack Lemmon realizes he left his wallet at home and wound up being the one who mugged Stallone.

But he was mistaken for a mugger and this was part of his issue, right?

It’s funny watching it now, because it’s so obviously Sylvester Stallone. So it’s amusing the whole role is just him being chased.

I agree with you and I found that throughout a lot of the stuff I was unearthing throughout this process.

In that, if he hadn’t become famous, I’d still look at him and think, “what an interesting looking dude,” and wonder what happened to him.

Speaking of that, there were times during “I Play Rocky,” knowing full well what happens in real life, and I’m still like, “Maybe just take the money. That’s a lot.”

It’s really remarkable. Especially when you convert the amount from what it was then to what it would be now.

I know you made a video for your audition which involved an old punching bag and gloves. What were you saying in it?

Oh, well, there was certain dialogue I was coming up with, or thinking of coming up with. And I hadn’t had my hands on too much of the script at this point. So I was just trying to capture his physicality and his movement as a boxer. I was just really passionate about the project. I wanted to put myself out there in a way. And, thankfully, I was able to get my hands on the script a bit later on.

So are you doing lines from “Rocky”? Or just stuff you came up with on your own?

I ask because that’s a time when you haven’t gained the weight yet, so you’re not in the physical condition you are when filming. So I feel you had to really sell this dialogue? Which obviously worked.

Yeah, I mean … it was difficult to come up with that part of it. I had given myself inspiration with some parts of the original film, and some parts from what I felt would work for dialogue from what I was understanding of the story. And then once I was able to get the script, then I was able to just put scenes on tape. And then continuously send them stuff until they relented.

Oh, there was more than one? You just kept going?

Well, that’s the spirit of this movie. Did you feel that way when you were sending them in? “Well, that’s what Stallone did.”

Hm … maybe? You know, it seems that way kind of now?

Right. But at that time, I was just like, “I probably seem crazy to everyone who is on the other end of this.”

Yeah, but I wasn’t thinking about that part for some reason, I guess.

Which is probably good, if you were getting ahead of yourself it doesn’t work out the way it did?

I know you spoke to Stallone before filming. A year ago, he was saying he knew nothing about this movie. When and how did that change?

Peter Farrelly tells a funny story about that. He had actually met with Stallone prior to that and discussed his level of involvement. And they discussed how Stallone would kind of not be necessarily in the trenches with us, just for the sake of Peter not wanting people to feel like Stallone had his hand in it in a way that it was shaped…

And historically Stallone never does that. I say that sarcastically because I’m well aware he has a specific vision for any movie he’s involved in…

Right. Right. So, Stallone went back after that and told somebody he has no idea about it. And Peter was like, “What are you doing?” And Stallone said, “You told me to separate myself.” And Peter was like, “Not that far, man!” So, I guess that was just a bit of a communication breakdown.

So in Stallone’s mind, he was doing a favor by saying that?

I’m not sure, but I was able to speak with him about a month before we started shooting. And I’m very grateful he was willing to take the time

What was that like? Was he in good spirits or was he apprehensive?

He was in great spirits about it. I was nervous, as you could probably imagine.

Yeah, and not only that, I had done so much of my own research. So, up to that point, it was really built up as this really big thing in my head. So, I was just really, really excited to meet him and to listen to him. He was really, really generous and disarming and very willing to share what that period of time was like for him.

What did he tell you that you don’t know already?

Oh, man. Well, he discussed with me building the character of Rocky as a writer. That’s where it became really interesting to me. Because he had studied filmmaking and writing while being an usher. So, hearing his perspective and his kind of clinical breakdown of how he approaches a script and of a character? It was hugely informative in developing and my understanding of this side of him as a writer.

From that, what changed on how you approached playing him? How does that conversation inform what we see?

You just really understand that this thing is his baby. And it really makes more sense that these numbers going so high during these negotiations because the script is that good. And so well written. Yeah, he’s a terrific writer and I think he proved that to Chartoff and Winkler with “Paradise Alley,” first.

My only experience with him was at the afterparty for “The Family Stallone.” He shows up at this restaurant in Little Italy and it’s like the Red Sea parting. Everyone stopped talking and made room so he could walk by. When he got near me I said, “Hey, Sly,” which I immediately regretted. He stopped, looked at me, and gave me a little nod.

He then walked off and I thought, “You know, good enough.”

Are you glad that you said it now? I feel like I would be.

But you keep bringing up meeting Wim Wenders. I know you’re a fan of his, is there something maybe happening?

I got to meet him at the Zurich Film Festival.

I know you like his movies, are you going to work with him?

I just think he makes great films, he’s made great films and he was a really, really sweet man and we got to speak. That’s pretty much it.

I feel that way about so many. Well, Scorsese obviously. Richard Linklater, Derek Cianfrance, Tim Burton.

That’s an eclectic group. “Place Beyond the Pines” and “Beetlejuice” are very different movies.

Very different movies. Well, I like that, You can go in so many different directions. And I appreciate directors and filmmakers who are singular.

And that is kind of the thing about Stallone, too. Did you look at the movies Stallone directed?

Honestly, well, I know he directed all the “Rocky” movies other than the first and fifth ones. And I understand he directed more stuff past that as well. But I hadn’t specifically looked at stuff he directed for this.

How far back did you go back to watch with Peter Farrelly’s films? Did you go back to “Dumb & Dumber”?

I’ve seen so much of his stuff already. So there’s not one that jumped out at me, but also, obviously, “There’s Something About Mary.”

It really is. I think he really killed it with that one. I mean, he has such an incredible sensibility. And he’s always aware of something on set. If there’s a moment to be discovered, to make a meal out of it, he’ll find it.

I always think about, “Unless someone comes up with six-minute abs.”

On social media a lot of people are doing their own “I Play …,” then insert any other Stallone movie type posts. If you had to play him again, what movie would you want to do?

Like, “I Play Cobra,” would be interesting. I do love “Cobra.”

You know, I guess I’m not the right age for this, but “I Play Rocky Balboa” would be very interesting…

Well, it’s the first one I remember. I would have had to have seen the ones prior? To the point I’m in the theater for “Rocky Balboa.”

Well, not necessarily. The first one I saw was “Rocky III”…

Because it was the one on cable all the time. Then I was told, “Oh, you know, the first one is a lot different.”

Yeah, I was pretty young, but I do remember seeing “Rocky Balboa.” And I just think there’s something interesting about the fact that, similar to how he’s fighting the boxing commission at the time to let him fight, because they think that he can’t, or shouldn’t — I think he was having a similar dialogue with the studio at the time. About him making the movie in the first place.

It’s interesting, even at that point, they still didn’t think they could take a chance on him making a “Rocky” movie.

I guess, yeah. It’s strange, but history does repeat itself.

Ah, OK, it’s not streaming, so it’s a little harder to find. It’s just interesting this is only a few years after “Rocky” and now he’s on stage singing with Dolly Parton. It’s kind of fascination what that one decision did for him…

It’s very true. And I think Dolly Parton is spectacular in that.

How good is she in that? Right? I mean, she has such a warmth to her. I mean, yeah. She’s just incredible in the movie and it makes it so fun. The two of them! They are dynamic.

You could also make “I Play Nick Martinelli.”

So what are the lessons you personally took away from playing Stallone? I can’t help but think there are lessons here for actors starting out.

I agree. Well, he really overcame so much and he didn’t have too many people in his corner at the time. I mean, thankfully, he had Sasha who was there for him, who AnnaSophia Robb plays in the movie. And she’s so great in it. And as much as you want to see Stallone persevere, and be kind of a lone wolf through this? For actors there’s meaning in that, and there’s a lesson to be learned in that.

But there’s also a lesson to be found in Sasha. Because you need that person sometimes in your life. Or sometimes it’s good to be that person for people — to remind people to believe in themselves. Because, no matter what, Stallone overcame so much, but of course he doubted himself. And if you don’t have at least somebody who is there, willing to be that person to remind you to believe in yourself, it’s a tough road.

Amazon MGM Studios will release “I Play Rocky” in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide on Friday, November 20.

#3593. Spider-Man’s Biggest Movie of All Time Officially Returns to Theaters in 1 Month

Marvel Cinematic Universe has regained its spark with releases like Spider-Man: Brand New Day and small-screen adventure like VisionQuest, The Punisher: One Last Kill, and Wonder Man. Each release brings us closer to Avengers: Doomsday, which will pit Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.)against the Avengers and even the X-Men. Fans are gearing up for the upcoming superhero mashup by revisiting the old titles for Easter Eggs and connective tissue. Series like Loki, along with Infinity War and Endgame, which elaborate on the multiversal connections, have returned to streaming charts.

The studio also released Avengers Endgame: Encore, an updated version by the Russo Brothers, which brought a plethora of new scenes that bridge the gap between the two features. Among the most recent titles, Tom Holland's Spider-Man: Brand New Day came out earlier this year and had an otherworldly reception. Fans were eager to see how Peter’s life fares after the events of No Way Home, and director Destin Daniel Cretton brought the right sensibilities to bring that story to life. Cretton brought a grounded, mature shift to Peter and touched upon the themes of the burden of adulthood and isolation that turn into a mutation within Peter.

We follow an adult Peter Parker, who lives a life of radical, self-imposed isolation. Because the spell erased the world's memory of his identity, he focuses entirely on being a full-time Spider-Man. Things take a turn when he faces a mysterious new threat: a telepathic villain capable of body-hopping and mind-control. As he transitions from a teenager, we find Peter as a self-reliant, gritty, street-level hero dealing with tactile, realistic hardships. The themes, performances, and Cretton’s vision made Brand New Day a record-breaking box office juggernaut, comfortably tracking as the highest-grossing film of 2026 and one of Marvel's biggest movies ever, having earned over $2.5 billion at the box office.

Now, before we see the ultimate clash between Doctor Doom and the Avengers, Marvel is bringing Brand New Day’s extended cut to the theaters. The new version has added between seven and 10 minutes of footage. Further, this footage will not be available on the Blu-ray release coming out next month, which doesn’t include any deleted scenes. The release seems similar to Spider-Man: No Way Home “More Fun Stuff Edition,” which added 11 minutes to the film that wasn’t on the home video release.

Check out Spider-Man: Brand New Day in theaters on December 4. Stay tuned to Collider for more such updates.

#3592. You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries

Starting today, the Gemini app’s “tasks” feature, previously known as Spark, is now available for free users after requiring AI Pro in the past.

Google previously referred to this capability as a 24/7 personal agent before integrating directly into the main Gemini app experience in October. Above the prompt box on mobile (or below on the web), you’ll see “Chat” and “Task.” The first option is the existing chatbot, while the latter lets you “hand off even more tasks to Gemini.”

With tasks, Google’s “goal is for Gemini to save you time and money.” Google shared use cases like:

With today’s announcement, Google is emphasizing that “Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because [your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards] already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere.”

Behind the scenes, Gemini tasks work in your own “hardware-isolated virtual machine” that’s sandboxed and has protections against prompt injection, while leveraging Google Safe Browsing when browsing the web.

Other safety features include having you confirm purchases and asking “clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous.”

Powered by the new Hydrogen model, free Gemini tasks are available in the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India.

#3591. Michael Dorn Hated Worf’s First Ever Star Trek Movie Scene: “You’re Making Him A Joke”

Worf's first scene in Star Trek Generations was a comedic moment that Michael Dorn hated and fought against doing.

After a prologue about Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner), Star Trek Generations introduces the crew from Star Trek: The Next Generation on the holodeck, where Worf is promoted to Lieutenant Commander aboard an 18th-century Enterprise. Worf is then forced to walk the plank, which Commander William Riker (Jonathan Frakes) orders removed, sending the Klingon into the ocean.

Appearing on The Show People Podcast, Michael Dorn shakes his head and admits, “I tried mightily not to do that scene," when host Andrew Keates asks him about Worf's infamous "remove the plank" moment. Dorn recalls meeting with Star Trek Generations' producers, who insisted that the scene was funny. Dorn lost the fight to have the scene removed, and Michael agreed to do the scene, but he still dislikes it over 30 years later:

Michael Dorn: “I didn’t think it was that funny. Here’s a guy, one of the most honorable… and you’re making him a joke.”

Watch the clip of Michael Dorn on The Show People Podcast below:

Using the holodeck was a novel way for Star Trek Generations to reintroduce Captain Jean-Luc Picard (Patrick Stewart) and the crew of the USS Enterprise-D to moviegoing audiences. Since Generations would end with the death of Captain Kirk, plus the off-screen deaths of Picard's family and the destruction of the Enterprise-D, Paramount and the producers wanted more comedy to balance out those losses.

However, Michael Dorn isn't wrong to feel that Worf's "remove the plank" scene turned the mighty Klingon into a joke. Sending Worf falling into the ocean was an unnecessary humiliation that didn't add anything to his character. Nor was there a payoff for Worf's promotion to Lt. Commander in Star Trek Generations. His new rank didn't factor into the movie's main story in any way.

Worf joined Star Trek: Deep Space Nine in season 4, but there was an idea making the rounds about Michael Dorn replacing Avery Brooks as series lead.

After Worf is dunked in the ocean (maybe or maybe not on purpose by Commander Riker), the Enterprise's Klingon has little to do in Star Trek Generations. Worf mostly disappears from the second half of the movie, besides appearing on the bridge when the Enterprise-D crash-lands on Veridian III.

Lt. Commander Worf would fare much better in the next film, Star Trek: First Contact, where the Klingon fights the Borg and utters his best movie dialogue, like "Assimilate this!" and telling Captain Picard, "If you were any other man, I would kill you where you stand!"

For Michael Dorn, Star Trek Generations wasted Worf and went out of its way to make the Klingon the butt of an unfunny joke.

Star Trek Generations is streaming on Paramount+
