#3590. Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles

40 years ago, the crime drama “Heat” opened in France and received positive reviews from Paris critics. No, not the “Heat” directed by Michael Mann that starred Robert De Niro and Al Pacino and would go on to become a revered classic — that came nine years later. The “Heat” that played in Europe in 1986 starred Burt Reynolds, was directed by multiple journeyman helmers, and was almost immediately forgotten only months after it limped into U.S. theaters in March of 1987.

American reviewers dismissed “Heat” with casual cruelty, but as so often happens in film history — think Jerry Lewis, Michael Cimino’s “Heaven’s Gate,” or Brian De Palma’s “Mission to Mars” — the French got our cinema right where our own critics got it embarrassingly wrong. “Heat,” in which Reynolds plays an aging mercenary held prisoner by a crippling gambling addiction, is not only one of Reynolds’ most interesting films but one of his most personal, and a top-tier entry in the canon of the subgenre that is “Burt Noir.” Related Stories Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: David Fincher’s Breezy Tarantino Spinoff Is a Disappointing Compromise Between Great Directors

From early on, one of the most interesting things about Burt Reynolds was the tension between his affable onscreen persona — the smiling, charming fellow who had major box office hits with crowd-pleasers like “Smokey and the Bandit” and “The Cannonball Run” — and the visible agitation simmering underneath. Reynolds was one of the premier talk show guests (and occasional guest hosts) of the 1970s and early 1980s, a guy who could always be counted on to tell a funny, self-deprecating anecdote that made the audience feel like a part of his inner circle.

But Reynolds always gave the sense that there was a chip on his shoulder — that he was mad about not being taken seriously enough, or being taken too seriously, or losing out on the best parts to his friend and competitor Clint Eastwood and other stars. (Never mind the fact that Reynolds lost out on most of his potentially successful roles — “Terms of Endearment,” “Die Hard,” “Pretty Woman” — because he turned them down, not because anyone took them from him.)

Early on, Eastwood let his controlled rage be a defining trait of his star persona; Reynolds generally tried, and failed, to cloak his under chuckling humility. Many of Reynolds’ best performances exploit this tension, from John Boorman’s “Deliverance,” in which Reynolds’ male bonding fishing expedition descends into a horror, to Paul Thomas Anderson’s “Boogie Nights,” in which the actor’s initially nurturing father figure turns dark and violent when tested.

Reynolds’ memoir, “But Enough About Me,” offers a fascinating glimpse into the contradiction between his healthy self-regard (hilariously exhibited in passages in which he disparages two of the best directors he ever worked with, Anderson and Peter Bogdanovich) and his persistent self-loathing (demonstrated in his candid appraisals of his many terrible personal and professional decisions). The latter informs an ongoing, if intermittent, cycle of Reynolds movies of which “Heat” is a key example: movies I define as “Burt Noir,” in which the actor plays supremely confident men of action tormented by regret and the knowledge that they’ve failed to live up to their potential.

The first, and possibly best, example of Burt Noir is the 1975 cop drama “Hustle,” in which Reynolds plays a Los Angeles detective surrounded by moral decay and corruption. Reynolds and director Robert Aldrich got to make “Hustle” after their commercial success with “The Longest Yard,” and they immediately squandered whatever mainstream goodwill that comedy had bought them with a film so grim and pessimistic it made James Ellroy look like Fred Rogers.

In “Hustle,” Reynolds is surrounded by evil both banal and terrifying, and he meets almost all of it with a weary resignation — aside from one desperate, possibly pointless act, he doesn’t even try to fight the men to whom he knows he is morally, intellectually, and physically superior. The movie reeks with sadness in spite of being marketed as a muscular action movie — though it is a muscular action movie, as is a later and more commercially successful Burt Noir, “Sharky’s Machine.”

That movie, in which Reynolds plays a cop who falls for the prostitute he’s got under surveillance, further explores the sense of moral outrage that marked “Hustle” and Reynolds’ directorial debut, “Gator,” and it gives Reynolds another of his tortured heroes who alternates between spurts of violent action and long passages of almost complete impotence — a combination that reaches its apotheosis in “Heat.”

A clue to what Reynolds is up to in terms of deconstructing his persona comes in the opening of “Heat,” a 12-minute prologue that doesn’t have much to do with the rest of the film other than breaking down Reynolds’ heroic image for audience members who still see him as a conventional leading man. Reynolds’ Nick Escalante tries to pick up a woman in a bar in the ugliest, aggressive way possible, and it’s confusing for the audience — why has the guy who was such a sweet charmer to Sally Field, Goldie Hawn, Jill Clayburgh, and Julie Andrews in earlier movies turned into such a misogynistic pig?

Even more confusing is what follows, when the meek twerp the woman is dating shows up and beats the hell out of Reynolds in the parking lot. We learn, later on, that the whole thing was a set-up — the guy hired Nick to fake everything so he could look like a hero in front of his girlfriend. But in the audience’s mind, the seed has already been planted; subconsciously we can never quite see this guy as a straightforward hero, and that’s the way Reynolds and screenwriter William Goldman want it.

The film progresses as a kind of hangout movie familiar to anyone who loves Quentin Tarantino’s “Jackie Brown” or “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth”; there’s a relatively solid genre movie structure running underneath everything, but Goldman takes plenty of time for character-developing digressions that give the whole movie a rich sense of melancholy texture.

Escalante’s tale of attempted moral redemption in the form of his efforts to help the victim of a sadistic young gangster avenge her beating moves from sharp wit (in the form of the best dialogue Goldman ever wrote — which is saying something when you’re talking about the guy who wrote “Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid”) and contemplative scenes of self-examination to shocking bursts of expertly choreographed violence and wistful romance.

It’s all given added layers of irony and resonance by the Las Vegas setting, which seems to mock Escalante’s dreams of hitting it big and escaping to a peaceful retirement in Italy, and Goldman’s choice to set the movie at Christmas, which only mocks Escalante more cruelly. Although “Heat” is one of Goldman’s least well known films (a movie that is easily forgotten amidst the more honored “All the President’s Men,” “Marathon Man,” and “Misery”), it’s one of his most beautifully written, with badinage as snappy as it is revealing and a weaving plot whose emotional effects really sneak up on you.

So why were American critics so dismissive? As is so often the case, they mostly seemed to be reviewing the chaotic circumstances of the production more than the movie that actually resulted from them. “Heat” was a famously troubled movie, whose misfortunes made their way into the press long before the film actually hit American screens. Its beginnings were auspicious: Goldman, one of the most respected writers in the business, was adapting his own novel (with a clause in his contract that said he couldn’t be rewritten), and Robert Altman was set to direct.

Then, only days before shooting, Altman quit the project after his favored cinematographer, Canadian cameraman Pierre Mignot, was denied an H-1 Visa to work in America. Altman claimed that over the course of eight pictures he had developed a style and way of working with Mignot that he didn’t want to abandon, and certainly didn’t want to have to reinvent in a matter of days with another director of photography. Whether or not this is the whole story is anybody’s guess — it was reported that the real reason Altman left had to do with creative differences between him and producer Elliott Kastner, and that Mignot merely gave him the excuse he was looking for to walk.

Goldman suggested Reynolds, who had helmed “Sharky’s Machine” and other fine pictures, take over directing himself, but Burt said he wanted to focus solely on his performance. Thus began a game of directorial musical chairs that would be widely reported and which gave “Heat” the patina of a disaster in the making. Reliable craftsman Dick Richards came on first, only to leave the production after getting into a fistfight with Reynolds on the set. In spite of lawsuits flying back and forth, Richards returned to the set, only to leave again when he fell off a camera crane and ended up in the hospital.

On the days when Richards was out second-unit director and stunt coordinator Stan Barrett took on directing duties, and some of the most electrifying moments in “Heat” can be attributed to him. Barrett had worked as Reynolds’ stunt double for more than 20 years and had a great sense of how to capitalize on the actor’s physicality and image, and the set pieces he directed for “Heat” — like a hotel room fight between Reynolds and some thugs — are beautifully staged and filled with brutally effective and original instances of sudden and shocking violence.

DGA rules at the time prohibited Barrett from taking over the reins for more than five days, since the guild forbade any preexisting member of a troupe from replacing the director — a rule, ironically, that was created when Reynolds’ friend Clint Eastwood fired director Philip Kaufman from “The Outlaw Josey Wales” and replaced him with himself. With only eight days of filming left on “Heat,” television stalwart Jerry Jameson (who had directed Reynolds years earlier on “Dan August”) stepped in and finished the picture.

The experience doesn’t seem to have been a happy one for many of the principals involved, especially Richards, who gave interviews begging people not to blame him for what he saw as the film’s failures. A DGA arbitration determined that Richards was responsible for 40% of the film — more than any of the other directors on the project — and thus should have the credit. Not wanting his name on the movie, Richards eschewed his usual credit for “Directed by R.M. Richards” and tried to wash his hands of the entire debacle as soon as he could.

With the movie’s own director badmouthing the film in the press, “Heat” never really stood a chance. Yet the movie that exists doesn’t show signs of any of the production’s dysfunction, aside from a slightly abrupt and abbreviated finale (one of several that was shot). In the end, Goldman and Reynolds, more than any director, are the true auteurs of “Heat,” and the consistency of their conception of Nick Escalante as an honorable, self-destructive, romantic, tortured, possibly doomed hero gives “Heat” a lingering emotional resonance and power that still works 40 years later.

Burt would continue his forays into Burt Noir both in film (“Malone,” “Rent-A-Cop,” “Physical Evidence”) and television (“B.L. Stryker,” “Hard Time”), but he never played this kind of character better than he did in “Heat.” The movie was remade, incidentally, in 2015 by “Con Air” director Simon West as “Wild Card.” That version didn’t connect with critics or audiences either, in spite of Goldman once again writing the screenplay. At this point it’s fair to assume that “Heat” is just a doomed project, which is a shame — since it also happens to represent one of Goldman’s finest artistic moments.

#3589. iCloud, App Store, and other Apple services hit by ongoing outage [U]

Apple services are having a rough Tuesday. iCloud, the App Store, and other services are experiencing an apparent outage, with users reporting connection failures and trouble signing in.

Downdetector is showing reports across multiple Apple services, even as Apple’s System Status page continues to list them as available.

Affected services include the App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay, Apple Support, iPhone Activation, and more.

Apple confirms a number of services experiencing issues on its general and developer status pages.

Apple retail stores and corporate offices are also reportedly experiencing outages.

Users are reporting unexpected iCloud sign-outs on iPhone and Mac, followed by verification failures or unknown errors when trying to sign back in.

Others say the App Store won’t load or download apps, while Apple Music and device activation are also running into problems. Developers have separately reported trouble accessing App Store Connect.

The number of "coincidental" system failure happening these days make it difficult to believe it's not cyberattacks, AI failures, or both. Even more suspicious is that they all seem to be reciting the same script for the cause: "an internal update".

The disruption follows last week’s widespread Microsoft Outlook outage.

Yesterday, banking services also experienced problems after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted online access and delayed some transactions involving other banks.

Are Apple services working for you? Let us know what you’re seeing in the comments.

Update: Apple now says an internal update caused the outage, ruling out a cyber attack, and many services are coming back online. Consumer-facing services are back online. Developer-focused services are still experiencing issues.

Apple: “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible." Company says this wasn’t a cyberattack.

#3588. The Google Wallet app is now available on iOS

Google Wallet is now available on iOS to “organize purchases, tickets, boarding passes, and more in one easy place” in the US.

The Google Wallet app on iPhone does not offer tap-to-pay functionality due to platform restrictions. Instead, Google touts three intended use cases:

App navigation is handled by a floating pill (in Liquid Glass) with two tabs. The homepage starts with a carousel of recent purchases slated for delivery, followed by boarding passes, and finally a grid of loyalty cards.

The next tab shows a list of recent transactions associated with Google. The Wallet app will display purchase emails and summarize them. You also get a list of Passes, which you can pin/unpin from the homepage, and payment methods saved to your Google Account.

The ‘plus’ FAB (floating action button) lets you add loyalty, gift, and payment cards (for use in Chrome). There’s a convenient “Everything else” camera scanner that can be used to digitize anything else.

The other main reason Google Wallet now exists on iOS is that the company wants the app to be a “secure hub for managing agentic purchases across Google.”

#3587. Why the Radical Lesbian Filmmaker Doc ‘Barbara Forever’ Deserves Oscar Recognition

Finally, a documentary as radical as the lesbian avant-garde feminist filmmaker it’s about. First-time feature filmmaker Brydie O’Connor’s Sundance-winning documentary “Barbara Forever” is a hypnotic archival collage that retraces the life, work, and death of Barbara Hammer.

The documentary, an early fall Strand release produced in partnership with Pamela Koffler and Christine Vachon’s recently Oscar-winning Killer Films, won in Park City for Matt Hixon’s editing. (Kristen Stewart also jumped on board as an executive producer.) It’s not hard to see why. “Barbara Forever” is an archival documentary that unfolds in the shape and style of its subject, an experimental filmmaker who put together some of the first publicly projected lesbian erotica actually made by a lesbian. Voiceover by the filmmaker spans her early career in the Bay Area (and halcyon days as an out lesbian), her 1992 feature debut “Nitrate Kisses,” and the final years of a cancer battle that ended in 2019. Related Stories Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break

Now New York-based, O’Connor centered her George Washington University thesis project on Hammer’s work before they’d ever met. “I read about Barbara and studied Barbara before I even saw her films,” O’Connor told IndieWire. She reached out to Hammer to “buy her DVDs because they weren’t showing anywhere in D.C. And she wrote back to me. At first, she was a little bit hard on me. She was like, ‘I see you’re writing from an edu.edu address. I just want to make sure that you’re actually a student because if you’re faculty, it would be much, much more expensive.’ [Laughs] And I said, ‘I promise, Barbara, I’m a student. I just can’t wait to see your movies.’ And she sent me her DVDs. So yeah, I think that initial impulse to explore her work was really about … ‘Why don’t more people know about Barbara and her work?'”

Hammer had degrees in psychology and literature before encountering “Meshes of the Afternoon” director Maya Deren’s films (which also influenced David Lynch) at San Francisco State in the 1970s. They lit the fuse for making her own movies. Circa that time, she’d been living in Santa Rosa and married to a man. She came out as a lesbian — busting through that closet, really, with abandon — and took off with her Super 8 camera to start making lesbian films. Growing up in Kansas, O’Connor, in her early 30s, resonated with Hammer’s early biography, and Hammer’s early lust for self-reinvention.

“She was not really tentative about anything. She picked up a camera in her late 20s as she was getting a divorce from a man when she realized that she was a lesbian and she made her film,” O’Connor said. “She learned by doing. And I was so inspired because, at the time, I was studying American studies and history in school. I had no background in the arts really, except for enjoying consuming them. And I really thought I would be a film critic or a writer… [Barbara Hammer] was not afraid to fail creatively. And she tried so many different ideas, of course, throughout her entire career in making over 85 films, but especially in that first decade of her career.”

Post-college and in New York, O’Connor, who’s spent “a decade in the Hammer world, and my entire adult consciousness,” would see Hammer at the Metrograph in Lower Manhattan. “I definitely was ‘the girl who wrote her thesis on Barbara,’ probably one of many, and I was day-playing in the film industry,” O’Connor said. “I would occasionally go up to Yale, where her formal archive is held, to continue doing independent research. I was looking at her love letters and her photographs… I wrote to her in January of 2019 when I was about to make my first short film. I said, ‘Hi, Barbara.’ I didn’t know how sick she was at the time. I was like, ‘I’m making my first film. Can I take you to coffee? Do you have any advice for me?’ And she wrote back to me and said, ‘I’m at the very, very end of my life, but best of luck with everything in your career.'”

Hammer died in March 2019, which is when O’Connor contacted the filmmaker’s partner, the human rights advocate Florrie Burke. “Florrie was the love of her life. They were together for 31 years,” O’Connor said. Their meeting culminated in O’Connor’s 2022 short film “Love, Barbara,” which she expanded into the feature that hit theaters this year. In a 2026 Oscar documentary race heavy on genocide and social issues — or a three-hour A24 movie that’s shaken up the entire form — “Barbara Forever” is life-affirming, lovely, yet still-important counter-programming.

The organic archival rhythm of “Barbara Forever” eschews talking heads altogether, instead conversing with what Hammer’s work looked and felt like. One of the film’s most charming snippets finds Hammer showing one of her (SFW!) films to a classroom of small schoolchildren. They end up having an unexpected appreciation for the experimental film clip’s non-narrative sensibilities.

O’Connor collaborated with Burke on sifting through 35 hours of audio recordings to stitch together a narration unfolding entirely in Hammer’s own words. “Florrie was so happy with [the short], but she always reminded me there’s so much more to Barbara than just our relationship,” O’Connor said. “Barbara’s this huge personality. She’s so charismatic and charming and really both thoughtful, but also very savvy. She wanted to be recognized. She wanted to be known for her work and her efforts, and she was uncompromising in what she made and how she shared her work. So it just made sense that she would be the narrator of the film.”

The Sundance-winning editing, too, proved a challenge, as O’Connor and her filmmaking team pored over more than 400 hours of visual material — from Hammer’s films, to outtakes, B-sides, home videos, and more. “I really wanted to convey with this film: Why did Barbara turn the camera on herself and her life and her lovers and her body as a method of alternative history making? What did she see in the value of that approach and then making experimental cinema out of it and demanding the value of that within culture?”

That Hammer’s work wasn’t more canonized during her life — an effort O’Connor has made partly her own, especially as a new digital restoration of “Nitrate Kisses” is making the rounds — isn’t only because of how confrontational she was about gender and her own sexuality. “Nitrate Kisses” is, after all, an experimental movie about lesbian repression dating back to the early 20th century. Is it also that autofiction and individualism, now a dominant mode of contemporary artistic expression, were also marginalized at that point within her particular corner of the art world?

“She was both an experimental filmmaker and avant-garde artist and a lesbian filmmaker. And she says, and this was something she said all throughout her life and career, that she didn’t fit neatly into either category where she could just build an audience within that space,” O’Connor said. “She really was uncompromising about being both and working at the intersection of both and having both audiences… The experimental film world didn’t necessarily want to see lesbian work, didn’t necessarily want to see the nude woman’s body on screen. And lesbians, there was not so much representation, especially in the ’70s, ’80s, ’90s, increasingly so, but her work was experimental and thought-provoking, and she felt like a lot of her queer audiences wanted more realistic depictions of queerness.”

O’Connor, who received a 2026 Creative Capital to not only finish her work on “Barbara Forever” but also continue making docs, said, “The industry is hard, but that certainly won’t stop me from making nonfiction films. I’m just excited to pivot to my next project.”

“Barbara Forever” is now available to stream on PVOD platforms.

#3586. The 8 Most Critically Acclaimed Books of All Time, Ranked

Critics have spent a long, long time debating which books deserve to be considered the greatest, with no end to their disagreements in sight. However, there are nevertheless a few consensus picks, classics that have been praised widely and for generations, pleasing both the public and reviewers, and influencing writers who followed.

These novels are the focus of this list. They are the true heavyweights of literary acclaim, the prize winners and centerpieces of the canon, still taught and discussed decades (or even centuries) after they were published.

"You could feel it: something terrible was going to happen." Critics flipped out over this one, immediately throwing around phrases like 'new Great American Novel'. Jonathan Franzen's masterpiece (although Freedom and Crossroads are pretty close) revolves around the Lambert family, whose elderly parents, Alfred and Enid, hope to gather their three adult children for one final Christmas together. However, each family member is struggling: professional disappointments, marital problems, financial troubles, deteriorating mental health.

One of The Corrections' greatest strengths is its extraordinary characterization. Franzen creates a family of deeply flawed individuals whose behavior can be infuriating, endearing, hilarious, and painfully recognizable, sometimes within the same paragraph. Tastemakers responded: the book won the National Book Award, and has since appeared on both the NYT 100 Best Books of the 21st Century list, as well as Time's All-Time 100 Novels.

"I am in here." One of the most analyzed novels of the 1990s, Infinite Jest is an ambitious, challenging, colossal book, clocking in at over 1000 pages, replete with sprawling digressions and nearly 100 pages of endnotes (which themselves have sub-notes). Set in a bizarre near-future society where corporations sponsor calendar years, the plot (such as it is) follows several interconnected characters and institutions, particularly a prestigious tennis academy and a nearby addiction recovery facility.

Meanwhile, a mysterious film known as Infinite Jest possesses such extraordinary entertainment value that viewers become incapable of doing anything except watching it (a prescient metaphor for the attention-consuming devices we all now carry around in our pockets). Several critics hailed the book on release, and even a few that were initially lukewarm about it declared it a classic in the years to follow.

"Caddy smelled like trees." William Faulkner has written several books that continue to be discussed and taught in literature courses around the globe, though perhaps the most well-regarded of them is The Sound and the Fury. It's a modernist landmark, chronicling the decline of the once-prominent Compson family in the South. The book is divided into four sections, each presenting a different perspective on the family's troubled history.

The first is narrated by Benjy Compson, a man with an intellectual disability, and the writing immerses us inside his fragmented perception of time. Subsequent sections explore the psychological struggles of his brothers Quentin and Jason, before the final portion zeroes in on the Compsons' Black housekeeper. Initially, all this received a muted reaction, but in the decades to follow, Faulkner was awarded the Nobel Prize, and this novel has placed highly on several publications' lists of the greatest novels ever.

"Call me Ishmael." Here, we meet Ishmael, a sailor who joins the crew of the whaling ship Pequod, commanded by the formidable Captain Ahab. However, Ahab has little interest in conducting an ordinary whaling expedition. Instead, he's consumed by an obsessive desire to kill Moby Dick, an enormous white sperm whale responsible for taking his leg during an earlier encounter. As the Pequod ventures across the oceans, Ahab's increasingly destructive obsession threatens to doom everyone aboard.

Although the main storyline may seem relatively straightforward, Moby-Dick is really a much more complicated, layered work. It incorporates philosophical reflections, elaborate symbolism, Biblical allusions, theatrical dialogue, and extensive discussions of whale anatomy and the whaling industry. These digressions can occasionally test readers' patience, but they're essential to the overall effect. Once again, this is a book that wasn't fully embraced on release, but nowadays, many consider Moby-Dick to be the Great American Novel.

"…remember that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice." This gem follows generations of the Buendía family in Macondo, a fictional Colombian settlement founded by José Arcadio Buendía and his wife, Úrsula Iguarán. Their marriage gives the early chapters much of their comedy and establishes a pattern that outlives them both. From here, Gabriel García Márquez weaves an expansive tale of magical realism, a cornerstone of the whole subgenre.

Indeed, the influence of One Hundred Years of Solitude is immense, with countless writers drawing inspiration from it. Authors such as Salman Rushdie, Toni Morrison, and Carlos Fuentes have all praised it, while Chilean poet Pablo Neruda famously called it "the greatest revelation in the Spanish language since Don Quixote." The book won a bevy of awards when it came out, and contributed to the author receiving the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature.

"So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past." A vivid time capsule of the Roaring Twenties, as well as a timeless statement on the promises and disappointments of the American Dream. The tale is told by Nick Carraway, a young bond salesman who becomes fascinated by his mysterious, fabulously wealthy neighbor, Jay Gatsby. Behind Gatsby's carefully cultivated persona lies an obsessive desire to reunite with Daisy Buchanan, a married woman he loved years earlier.

What might have been a glamorous romance instead develops into a devastating examination of wealth, class, ambition, and the impossibility of reclaiming the past. There is so much wisdom and bittersweet emotion here, despite the book's relatively modest length of 180 pages. When The Great Gatsby was first published, peers like T.S. Elliot and Gertrude Stein praised it. Today, it appears on countless 'greatest novels' lists and is taught in high schools all over the world.

"There is no greatness where there is not simplicity, goodness, and truth." This one is so highly regarded worldwide that its title is sometimes used as a shorthand for literary excellence. Set against the Napoleonic Wars, War and Peace follows several aristocratic Russian families as they become entangled with some of the most consequential events in European history. The cast includes the idealistic Pierre Bezukhov, the disillusioned Prince Andrei Bolkonsky, and the spirited Natasha Rostova.

Each of these characters undergoes a profound personal transformation over the course of the book. Through their experiences, Tolstoy explores everything from love and mortality to the nature of history and the forces that shape human destiny. It's remarkable that he's able to nimbly combine all these elements. Indeed, his prose moves effortlessly between lavish aristocratic gatherings, devastating battlefield scenes, and quiet moments of introspection, making for a detailed portrait of Russian society.

"History, Stephen said, is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake." Many regard this cryptic, boundary-pushing book to be the greatest English-language novel of the 20th century. Taking place over a single day in Dublin, June 16, 1904, Ulysses centers on three characters: Leopold Bloom, an advertising salesman; Stephen Dedalus, a young intellectual; and Molly Bloom, Leopold's wife. Their seemingly ordinary experiences form the foundation of an extraordinarily ambitious literary experiment, loosely modeled on Homer's 'Odyssey'.

Rather than depicting heroic adventures, writer James Joyce transforms everyday encounters, mundane activities, and private thoughts into an epic exploration of human consciousness. The prose itself conveys this. The author employs a dizzying assortment of narrative techniques, including stream of consciousness, elaborate wordplay, parody, and radical stylistic experimentation. Not for nothing, many literary heavyweights have declared Ulysses to be a masterpiece, including Faulkner, Hemingway, and T.S. Eliot.

Toni Collette and Kit Harington are shooting a new Miss Marple and 20th Century has several more Christies in development, so the drawing room is busier than it has been in decades. Here is which of them you are, and the case for yours being the best.

Order, method, and a quiet confidence that you are the cleverest person present. Poirot is a retired Belgian police officer who solves murders by sitting still and thinking, and who is vain enough to make the reveal a performance every single time.

People tell you things because they cannot imagine you being a threat. Marple solves murders by comparing everybody to somebody she once knew in St Mary Mead, which sounds like a joke until you notice it works every time, because human beings are not as original as they think.

You have far too many ideas and roughly a fifth of them are excellent. Ariadne Oliver is a successful crime novelist who is sick of her famous foreign detective and keeps saying so, which is Christie writing about Christie and getting away with it completely.

You are steady, decent and the reason the difficult genius has anybody at all. Hastings narrates the early Poirot novels, misses most of the clues, and is the only character in the books that Poirot is unambiguously fond of, which tells you what he is really for.

#3585. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3583. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3582. OpenAI upgrades ChatGPT and Codex with new GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models

OpenAI kicked off the GPT-6 generation with Astra in September, then upgraded Sol to GPT-6.1 a few weeks later at DevDay.

Today, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are coming to ChatGPT Work and Codex together. OpenAI says both can finish demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done before hitting your usage limit.

Astra is still the model OpenAI recommends for your hardest projects.

Say you have a screenshot of a slide and want the rest of your presentation to look like it. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra can use that screenshot as a template and match the layout, colors, and even the font size.

On the Codex side, OpenAI says Astra is better at making and testing changes in an existing project.

“Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision,” OpenAI says.

Sol is the more affordable model for everyday coding and writing, and it gets surprisingly close to Astra on one coding test.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.

Some of you have been asking very politely. Some of you have just been asking.GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available.Super efficient and built to perform where it counts—the real world.https://t.co/qr2iP0GpfX pic.twitter.com/jLCyVIws2Y

Both models are available starting today in ChatGPT Work and Codex on Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu.

The $200/month Pro plan also gets Ultrafast mode for the first time with Sol. The $500/month Pro plan gets Ultrafast on both models, as do eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces once an admin enables it.

How fast is Ultrafast? OpenAI says it can generate tokens at up to 4.5 times the standard rate on either model, although it uses more of your allowance. You can switch speeds from the model picker.

Developers can use both models through the API today as well. Astra’s standard input and output prices are 20% lower than with GPT-6 Astra, while Sol keeps its GPT-6.1 pricing.

You can read more in OpenAI’s full announcement.

#3581. Fall Festival Movies Sold: Magnolia Heaps Dollars on ‘Trash Mountain’ with Caleb Hearon and Zooey Deschanel

This year’s TIFF and Venice were quieter in terms of breakout sales, especially when compared to last year’s splash for “Obsession,” and several awards contenders were scooped up before they even premiered at the festival. But other smaller buyers have emerged in recent weeks to release some of the more critically acclaimed titles that didn’t land major sales ahead of time.

The festivals are long done, but we’re still tracking every sale that happens, so check back frequently.

Distributor: MagnoliaDirector: Kris ReyFestival: TIFF CentrepieceBuzz: Not unlike Jordan Firstman going from comedian to unexpected leading man and festival circuit darling, Caleb Hearon earned some praise for his leading man turn in “Trash Mountain,” a dark comedy he wrote and starred in along with Zooey Deschanel that grapples with grief and growing up. Kris Rey directed the film that premiered at TIFF and was produced by “Jurassic World” filmmaker Colin Trevorrow. The film also stars Jacki Weaver, Jaboukie Young-White, and Kyle Marvin and was co-written by Ruby Castor. Curiously, Lilly Wachowski was at one point attached to direct the film before Rey came aboard. Magnolia now is planning a theatrical release in 2027. Related Stories Bill Hader’s Feature Directorial Debut ‘They Know’ Lands at Black Bear Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation

Distributor: Kino LorberDirector: Maiken BairdFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: This documentary about Palestinian-American author and intellectual Edward Said earned strong reaction in its premiere at TIFF and festivals like NYFF and IDFA, in part because though he’s been dead for over 20 years, his writing and his views have been far more relevant in a post-October 7 landscape. IndieWire’s review out of TIFF praised the construction of the documentary and how it manages to be decades-spanning and comprehensive in a manageable running time. And Anne Thompson spoke with the filmmakers about the challenges of making the documentary and the fear that it being about Palestine would pose barriers to a distributor stepping up to buy it. Thankfully, Kino Lorber did just that, and it will be planning a theatrical release for 2027.

Distributor: Cohen Media GroupDirector: May el-ToukhyFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: Venice’s top prize winner of the Golden Lion has found a U.S. deal, this one made out of AFM with Cohen Media Group. Not only did el-Toukhy (“Queen of Hearts,” “The Crown”) movie win the Golden Lion this year, star Mathilde Arcel also won the Volpi Cup for Best Actress. The Danish film, also Denmark’s official Oscar selection, is a period drama set after World War II about a former housekeeper now set to be married to the household’s wealthy patriarch. But as she plans an extravagant dinner party to celebrate the occasion, hidden aspects of her past begin to resurface. Namely, it has to do with Danish witch hunts of those associated with Nazis after the war, and our positive review called it an “angry, despairing film” with a “Haneke-level bleakness in its assessment of human nature.” Cohen Media Group also recently bought an Isabelle Huppert comedy called “All About Corinne” that played at TIFF and premiered at Locarno.

Distributor: Sony Pictures ClassicsDirector: Niki ByrneFestival: TIFF Special PresentationsBuzz: Sony Pictures Classics have acquired all rights in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore) to “The Julia Set,” written and directed by Niki Byrne. The film had its world premiere at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival and follows a gifted young math prodigy (“One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti) who is “recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics, while at the same time falling into a romantic relationship with her charismatic teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney).”

Distributor: Strand ReleasingDirector: Hanaël El YousfiFestival: TIFF DiscoveryBuzz: This directorial debut follows two friends, one Muslim and one Jewish, spending a carefree summer in Marseille, only to see the expectations and tensions between their traditional families start to get in the way of their friendship and leads them to take hold of their own destinies. El Yousfi both wrote and directed the feature, co-writing it with Raphaël Chevènement and Mia Grace Brown. It had its international premiere at TIFF, but it actually had a small bow at a French festival called the Angoulême Francophone Film Festival, where it won an Audience Award and a Special Prize for its cast. “The Daughters of Abraham” first opens in France on December 30. But Strand, a Culver City-based distributor behind recent releases like Mexico’s Oscar submission “On the Road,” “In a Whisper,” and the 4K restoration of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin,” will release it in North America in 2027.

Distributor: Black BearDirector: Nahnatchka KhanFestival: TIFF MarketBuzz: This market title is a rom-com starring an indelible trio of Greta Lee, Rebecca Ferguson, and Carrie Coon, and it wrapped production in September. Read more about the film here.

Distributor: 1-2 SpecialDirector: Jacqueline LentzouFestival: Venice OrizzontiBuzz: This Greek coming-of-age story won filmmaker Jacqueline Lentzou the Best Director prize in the Horizons section of the Venice Film Festival, but 1-2 Special picked it up after its North American premiere at NYFF and head of additional screenings at BFI London Film Festival, the Chicago International Film Festival, and the Busan International Film Festival. Blending what the release describes as both the “cosmic and the mundane,” the film follows a 15-year-old girl who meets a new classmate named Phaedra but also begins to notice signs and symbols from a dream world surfacing around her, ultimately leading her to an ethereal transformation. This is Lentzou’s second feature after 2021’s “Moon, 66 Questions.” 1-2 Special is planning a theatrical release for 2027.

Distributor: Sony PicturesDirector: Roshan SethiFestival: TIFF CentrepieceBuzz: This action-thriller starring Michelle Yeoh as a surgeon who is abducted and forced to operate on a mysterious patient is a bit of a departure for Sethi. Sethi’s previous film was the charming rom-com “A Nice Indian Boy,” and he’s also the co-creator of the medical drama “The Resident.” But reviews for the film were solid, and it’s not typical for the majors to buy festival titles, but Sony is already dating it for release on April 2, 2027.

Distributor: Universal Pictures and Blumhouse Atomic MonsterDirector: Joshua GiulianoFestival: TIFF Midnight MadnessBuzz: IndieWire first broke the news about the film originally set up at the Independent Film Company and Shudder being picked up by Universal and Blumhouse Atomic Monster for a deal that could surpass $10 million as the companies hope to find the next “Obsession,” just as they did last year. Read more here.

Distributor: HBO Documentary FilmsDirector: Rebecca HunttFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: “Rapinoe” about US Women’s National Soccer star Megan Rapinoe was the opening night documentary at TIFF. Rapinoe was in attendance at the premiere screening of director Rebecca Huntt’s (“Beba”) film, which grapples more with Rapinoe’s progressive politics, such as her kneeling in solidarity with Colin Kaepernick, and her coming out story, than it does on the stories from her soccer career about how she led the US Women’s team to two World Cup titles, an Olympics Gold, and the Ballon d’Or. HBO Documentary Films has North American TV and streaming rights to the film. THR first reported the news.

Distributor: Roadside Attractions and VerticalDirector: Lauren Miller RogenFestival: TIFF Gala PresentationBuzz: Lauren Miller Rogen directs her husband Seth Rogen alongside Anna Kendrick and Kate Berlant in this comedy about parenthood and prospective parenthood. It follows a childless couple who begin debating the merits of having kids when their divorced friend and her child move in with them. The cast is stacked, including Issa Rae, Dan Stevens, Zach Cherry, Ed Helms, Ashley Park, Sharon Stone, and David Strathairn in supporting parts.

“Babies” is described as heartfelt and poignant in what is shaping up to be a strong year for Seth Rogen. The movie launched sales at TIFF nearly a year to the date prior to its Roy Thomson Hall premiere. The distributors are planning for a release in early 2027.

Distributor: Focus FeaturesDirector: Simon StoneFestival: Telluride and TIFFBuzz: Andrew Scott is said to be fantastic in this performance based on the true story of “Chariots of Fire” and “Gandhi” star and thespian Ian Charleson, who died of AIDS at the age of 40 but managed to raise awareness for the epidemic after his death. Focus has already dated the film for late November, the same time slot it gave “Hamnet” last year.

Distributor: NetflixDirector: Danny BoyleFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: The opening night film for this year’s Biennale, “Ink” is the story of the birth of The Sun tabloid in the ’60s and the collaboration between editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) and Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) that made it the notorious publication it is today. Netflix didn’t acquire worldwide rights to the film, so it could easily be something it sees as both commercial and an awards play.

#3580. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 Pro (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3579. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3577. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

#3576. The Odyssey’s First Big Box Office Record Beaten By New Mckenna Grace Sci-Fi Movie

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is dawning with a major box office record already under its belt.

The movie, which was helmed by longtime franchise director Francis Lawrence, is the sixth installment in the Hunger Games franchise and the second prequel. In this case, it follows the 50th annual games, in which Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) competed when he was a teenager. The character is played by Woody Harrelson in the timeline of the original four movies. The star-studded ensemble cast of 2026's Sunrise on the Reaping also includes Mckenna Grace, Glenn Close, Ralph Fiennes, Kieran Culkin, Ben Wang, Whitney Peak, Maya Hawke, Iris Apatow, Elle Fanning, and Jesse Plemons.

Per Deadline, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping has taken in $21.25 million in previews at the domestic box office on Thursday. Not only does this mark the best preview gross for a Hunger Games movie since the second installment, 2013's Catching Fire ($25.2 million), it sees the movie beating the $17.6 million previews of Christopher Nolan's record-breaking epic The Odyssey. At the time, The Odyssey had the best preview grosses of the year. So far, it has only been surpassed by Spider-Man: Brand New Day ($72 million) and Sunrise, giving the latter the second-biggest previews of 2026 year-to-date.

There is at least one remaining 2026 movie that is expected to have bigger previews than Sunrise on the Reaping, namely the Marvel Cinematic Universe's Spider-Man: Brand New Day follow-up Avengers: Doomsday. However, other strong contenders include Dune: Part Three and Jumanji: Open World. Regardless, Sunrise on the Reaping's performance is remarkable. Below, see how it compares to the previous Hunger Games movies:

The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 1 (2014)

The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 2 (2015)

The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023)

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (2026)

It is worth noting that, while this chart is not adjusted for inflation, every installment in the franchise except the original has debuted in the same pre-Thanksgiving frame, making them especially comparable. Not only has Sunrise on the Reaping reversed the downward trend that the franchise has been experiencing since 2014, it has brought it back up to nearly the same level as Catching Fire, which remains the highest-grossing installment.

While preview numbers are not always a reliable predictor of a movie's ultimate performance, if the new installment has a similar trajectory to Catching Fire (which it could - Sunrise on the Reaping reviews have earned it a Verified Hot audience score of 95% on Rotten Tomatoes, improving upon Catching Fire's 89% and marking the best of the franchise), it could ultimately open to $133.3 million (the third-best debut of the franchise) and gross $733.5 million worldwide (the third-best overall haul as well).

Critics have given Sunrise on the Reaping 68% on the Rotten Tomatoes Tomatometer, which is the fifth-best for the franchise ahead of Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.

Should The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping climb that high by the end of its run (against a reported budget of roughly $200 million), it will reestablish the franchise as a major player in the box office arena. In fact, if it does debut above $100 million, it will be the first Lionsgate movie to do so since Mockingjay – Part 2 11 years ago (though they got close with the smash hit Michael Jackson biopic Michael, which earned a 3-day debut of $97.2 million).

#3575. The 10 Best Action War Movies of All Time, Ranked

There’s a risk with making a war movie also feel like an action one, especially if a filmmaker wants to have things feel anti-war, and sure, most war movies should be at least a little anti-war, otherwise they might run the risk of feeling like propaganda. If it’s a fictional war, or if it’s something that really rewrites history, and it’s all done well, then maybe it’s okay to have some fun with the war genre, though.

The following movies do it well, and differ from the likes of Platoon, Saving Private Ryan, and Das Boot, all of which have moments of combat and tension, but are a little harder to label as “action movies” in the traditional sense. These are the best action war movies of all time, and an “action war movie” is just what you'd expect: something that belongs to both of those genres (and maybe one or two others at the same time, too).

Even though John Woo is one of the all-time greatest action movie directors, he’s also so prolific that certain movies in his filmography tend to get a bit overlooked, especially those without gunfights, which is the style of action he’s best known for. If only this were an opportunity to rave about Last Hurrah for Chivalry, but alas, that’s “just” a martial arts movie, and it doesn’t really have anything that makes it qualify as a war film as well.

But hey, at least there’s Red Cliff, which does have tons of hand-to-hand fighting, thanks to its historical setting, but it’s all on a much bigger scale than Last Hurrah for Chivalry. You do have to watch both parts of Red Cliff to fully appreciate it, naturally, though if you want one singled out, may as well make it the first part, released in 2008 (the second part from 2009, Kill Bill-style, is a little slower-paced and maybe not quite as impressive with its action).

Calling Black Hawk Down realistic as far as its historical accuracy is concerned might be questionable, but calling it realistic in terms of how it captures relatively modern-day combat isn't out of the question. Or maybe grounded and visceral are slightly better words to use to describe how Black Hawk Down feels, because the film depicts the Battle of Mogadishu, and pretty much refuses to let up pacing-wise once said battle begins.

That does mean Black Hawk Down is exhausting, but with a purpose. It dramatizes (and takes some liberties with) an actual event, and feels grittier with its presentation than so many other war films made around the same time, or before, or since… or, well, any time, really. And for what it’s worth, there’s a pretty impressive ensemble cast here, especially with some who became more famous in the years following 2001.

High-concept premises don’t get much higher than the one found in G.I. Samurai, and the commitment to that premise is admirable. It’s a time travel movie that involves soldiers from the 20th century going back to samurai times. While there, they inevitably have to fight in a very different sort of combat, concerning samurai battles (it’s in the title and stuff) of the sort fought in the 15th and 16th centuries in Japan.

Speaking of things being in the title, it’s nice when a movie doesn’t lie to you, and you know what you're in for with just a couple of words. There are G.I. soldiers and there are samurai, and they fight. That is G.I. Samurai. It’s a good time, featuring plenty of action and technically being a mash-up of two different sorts of war movies at the same time, thanks to the time travel angle.

It’d be easiest to describe Wings as a World War I melodrama with quite a bit of romance as well, thanks to it having a love triangle at its center, but there is still action here. For something that’s now very close to a century old, it’s quite remarkable to behold, with the dogfighting sequences being some of the best parts of the movie, and the parts that hold up the best all this time later.

For something that’s now very close to a century old, it’s quite remarkable to behold, with the dogfighting sequences being some of the best parts of the movie.

Also, Wings was the first movie to win Best Picture at the first Academy Awards ceremony, though it didn’t set a precedent for such movies (like, those partly belonging to the action genre) to win that award often. And it won alongside another 1927 release, Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans, with Wings getting "Outstanding Picture" and the latter getting the unique and soon-to-be-retired award of "Unique and Artistic Picture." Both are romances, but very different kinds of romance films. Anyway, if you're into older movies, Wings, though not perfect, is still a must-watch.

Since it’s set the year after the Vietnam War ended, Eastern Condors kind of gets around being a Vietnam War movie of sorts that proves bombastic and entertaining, in contrast to most Vietnam War movies, which play up the horror, misery, and moral complexities of the conflict. The premise involves prisoners getting the option of being excused, a little like another action/war movie from 1967, and that’ll be mentioned shortly.

But a good premise is a good premise, so that’s okay. Here, the characters go into Vietnam and undertake a dangerous mission to destroy missiles that U.S. forces abandoned there. When there, lots of shootouts and then even some hand-to-hand fight scenes ensue. Eastern Condors is maximalist, and then it’s also remarkably generous with just how much action it features throughout (almost exhausting, but in a good way).

Four years on from Black Hawk Down, Ridley Scott made another war movie with Kingdom of Heaven, but it’s worth mentioning both, since the two do have quite a bit by way of action and spectacle. As for differences, though, this one goes back much further in time, since Kingdom of Heaven takes place during the Crusades, with the plot following a blacksmith who gets swept up in the complicated and alarmingly large-scale war.

There’s intrigue here and political drama alongside all the battle sequences, and if you watch the director’s cut (much better than the theatrical cut), the non-action stuff is quite compelling, too. But if you're after action and battles, that side of Kingdom of Heaven does shine bright, since Ridley Scott, though not the most consistent of filmmakers, can generally helm this kind of movie better than the vast majority of well-known directors out there.

John Woo is back here, on this ranking, with Bullet in the Head being a bit more of a classic kind of John Woo film compared to Red Cliff. Like, it’s got shootouts, basically. But then it differs a little from some of his other heroic bloodshed movies because it gets arguably even darker than the likes of A Better Tomorrow and The Killer (Hard Boiled is just a blast, though… violent, sure, but mostly fun).

Bullet in the Head is more despairing because the lead characters end up fleeing Hong Kong, and find that it makes their experiences worse, since they end up entangled in the Vietnam War. It begins as a crime film, and becomes a Vietnam War film. And then all the while, whichever genre it’s focusing on, it retains a pretty high level of action throughout. If you don’t mind watching something a bit depressing, it’s very much worthwhile.

While all the other action movies Michael Mann’s directed can be called crime/thriller films as well as action-related, The Last of the Mohicans very much isn’t a crime film, and it stands out among the other Michael Mann action films for taking place so long ago. It’s set during the 18th century, and the conflict everything plays out against is the French and Indian War, which involved the British Empire, the French Empire, and certain Native American tribes.

It’s a real blend of genres for something that clocks in at under two hours, given it also works as something of a war and adventure film, and romance is pretty central to the narrative, too. The Last of the Mohicans could've stood to be a little longer, because it’s like an epic movie just without the epic runtime, but at least what is here is remarkable, and honestly pretty difficult to fault.

The Dirty Dozen was alluded to earlier, back when talking about Eastern Condors, since they share that whole basic premise of “Hey, you shady guys doing this really dangerous thing that might kill you all, but if you survive, your crimes will be pardoned.” It has a remarkable cast and is very well-structured as an action/adventure/war movie, with the mission taking place in the final act, and said mission involving going behind enemy lines during World War II.

Before that final act, things are still exciting and interesting, but there is a lot of set-up and character development (developing some very eccentric characters at that, too). The Dirty Dozen is quite fun for something ultimately rather dark and intense, with an odd sort of tone struck here, yet the movie thankfully makes it work. And it all packs a fairly solid punch even close to six decades on from its release.

Yeah, so it’s not historically accurate, of course, but Braveheart does have a ton of action, and it also builds into something of a war movie as it goes along (like Wings, it was a Best Picture winner, too). It begins as a movie about revenge, but that quest for revenge ultimately balloons into something much grander, and that’s when all the war and battle scenes really come into it.

William Wallace (a real person, but again, this film’s not exactly a biopic) is the central character here, and he ends up inspiring a rebellion – and leading an army – in the wake of getting violent revenge against some English soldiers responsible for the death of the woman he loved. Those are the basics. And Braveheart isn't quite basic, but it almost is. It’s straightforward, yet works incredibly well for what it is, and the spectacle here is something to behold.
